cuisine: Modern Shojin / plant-forward vegetable cuisine
hours_raw: 11:00–22:00 daily (L.O. 21:00); lunch 11:00–14:00, cafe/tea 14:00–17:00, dinner 17:00–22:00. Shop/deli 11:00–20:00. Inside Tokyo Midtown Hibiya 2F; closures follow the building's schedule.
gf_detail: The kitchen advertises gluten-free options "on request" (per THREE's official page and Tabelog), and there are genuinely rice-based, wheat-free building blocks: the winter-vegetable frittos (フリット) are coated in a 米粉・豆腐の衣 (rice-flour + tofu batter, not wheat tempura batter), and there are rice mains (十穀米/玄米雑穀ご飯). BUT this is NOT a dedicated GF kitchen — it is a shared plant-based kitchen, so a celiac must confirm each dish. Concrete wheat risks found on the menu: the soy-milk tantanmen (豆乳担々麺) is a wheat-noodle dish; taco rice uses seasoned "veggie-meat" that commonly contains soy sauce/wheat; miso and standard shoyu-based seasonings (tomato miso, dressings) are wheat-fermented unless a wheat-free tamari is confirmed; no dedicated fryer is documented so the フリット and any fried item risk shared-oil cross-contact. Treat as "real GF items exist, but confirm ingredients + cross-contamination for each order" rather than safe-by-default.
vegan_detail: The whole restaurant is meat- and fish-free ("MODERN SHOJIN"), and there is a clearly fully-vegan flagship: the seasonal ベジミールスタンド / veggie-meal stand (~¥4,290) — e.g. Brussels-sprouts borscht, shiitake soy-milk gratin, celeriac steak with romesco, root-vegetable terrine, kale & Puy-lentil salad. Other plant-based items: ten-grain veggie-meat taco rice (¥1,980), tomato-miso soy-milk tantanmen (¥2,200), spiced carrot cake, soy-milk-&-turmeric whipped desserts. HOWEVER the menu is not uniformly vegan — THREE's official page states some items contain eggs and dairy, so a vegan must specify and check per dish. Dashi: the set includes a 冬野菜のすまし汁 (vegetable clear soup); sources do not explicitly confirm it is 100% plant-based (no bonito), so flag/ask about hidden dashi. Soy milk is used widely as the dairy substitute; no egg noted in the vegan meal stand itself.

cultural_comfort.note: Inside Tokyo Midtown Hibiya, a flagship shopping/dining complex 2 min from Hibiya Station in the Ginza/Yurakucho tourist core. Tabelog lists a multilingual (English) menu, and staff are used to international customers. A foreign diner asking about vegan/GF in English can expect to be understood, though precise allergen cross-contamination questions are still best confirmed carefully.

chef_bio.background: REVIVE KITCHEN THREE is the restaurant arm of the Japanese natural cosmetics brand THREE (by ACRO), not a single-chef establishment. Its 'EAT BEAUTY, LIVE BEAUTY' concept extends the brand's plant-based skincare philosophy into food.
chef_bio.philosophy: MODERN SHOJIN — reinterpreting traditional meat/fish-free Buddhist shojin cooking with international techniques and seasonal domestic vegetables; guided by 地産地消 (local production, local consumption) and 身土不二 (body and land are one).
chef_bio.specialty: Seasonal plant-based vegetable platters/meal stands and natural wine.

gf_cross_contamination: Shared plant-based kitchen, not a dedicated GF facility — confirm each dish.
No dedicated fryer documented; フリット/fried items may share oil.
Wheat-noodle tantanmen prepared in the same kitchen.
Miso and standard shoyu seasonings are wheat-fermented unless wheat-free tamari confirmed.
soy_sauce_wheat: Taco rice 'veggie meat' and various seasonings likely use wheat-based soy sauce/miso — confirm wheat-free tamari before ordering as GF.
vegan_cross_contact: Menu is not fully vegan — some items contain egg/dairy per official page; specify vegan.
Vegetable clear soup (すまし汁) dashi not confirmed bonito-free — ask.
staff_allergy_handling: Official page and Tabelog both state vegan and gluten-free options are available on request, indicating staff will accommodate — but they market 'options', not certified allergen-safe preparation.
positives: Entirely meat- and fish-free menu.
Multiple genuinely rice-flour / rice-based (wheat-free) components.
A clearly fully-vegan flagship meal stand.
Central, English-friendly location used to dietary requests.

cuisine: 山菜蕎麦 (mountain-vegetable soba)
hours_raw: Not verified — no official website, Tabelog, or listing could be found for this establishment.
gf_detail: UNVERIFIED. Despite an extensive search (Tabelog, Gurunavi, HotPepper, Retty, Ikyu, Michelin, dedicated GF-soba guides, and Japanese GF blogs), no website, menu, or listing for こうち山菜 could be located, so its advertised "グルテンフリー対応" claim cannot be confirmed and a celiac must NOT rely on it. Treat as 'ask' until confirmed in person or by phone. General soba-shop wheat risks that almost always apply and must be asked about: (1) most Japanese soba is nihachi (二八, 80% buckwheat / 20% wheat flour) — only certified 100% juwari (十割) is candidate GF, and even juwari carries wheat cross-contamination from shared water/boards/flour dusting, so it is 'ask' at best, not GF; (2) the tsuyu/dipping broth is normally made with regular soy sauce (醤油), which contains wheat; (3) tempura for sansai toppings uses wheat batter and, in a small shop, a shared fryer. Confirm in Japanese: 十割そばですか？（100% buckwheat?）小麦は使っていますか？（any wheat?）つゆの醤油は小麦不使用ですか？（wheat-free soy sauce?）
vegan_detail: UNVERIFIED — no menu could be found. A sansai (山菜, wild mountain vegetable) soba is plant-forward on its toppings, but the default soba broth (tsuyu/kake-jiru) in virtually every Japanese soba shop is built on katsuo-dashi (bonito) and/or niboshi, so it is NOT vegan unless a kombu-only broth is specifically prepared. Hidden animal risks to ask about: bonito/fish dashi in the broth, and mirin/egg in some batters. Confirm in Japanese: 出汁は鰹や煮干しを使っていますか？（bonito/fish stock?）昆布だしにできますか？（kombu-only possible?）

cultural_comfort.note: No online presence found; assume a small local Japanese-only shop with little to no English. A foreign celiac/vegan diner should bring written Japanese allergy cards or a Japanese-speaking companion. Verify the establishment exists before routing anyone here.

gf_cross_contamination: Unverified establishment — no data. Standard small-soba-shop risks to assume until confirmed: shared boiling water and cutting boards between wheat-blended (nihachi) and any 100% (juwari) soba; flour dusting on work surfaces; wheat-based tsuyu (soy sauce); shared tempura fryer with wheat batter for sansai toppings.
soy_sauce_wheat: Assume standard wheat-containing soy sauce (醤油) in the tsuyu unless the shop confirms a wheat-free tamari.
vegan_cross_contact: Assume bonito/fish (katsuo) dashi in the broth unless a kombu-only stock is confirmed.
staff_allergy_handling: Unknown — no listing found to assess.

cuisine: Ramen (vegetable / vegan-and-gluten-free-aware)
hours_raw: 9:00–23:00 (L.O. 22:30), open year-round / no fixed closed day. Note: vegan items served from ~10:00; the 貝塩らーめん (clam-salt, bonito-based) is a limited 40 servings from 14:00.

hours.notes: Last order 22:30. Open all year, no regular closing day. Vegan menu from ~10:00; clam-salt ramen (contains bonito) limited to 40 servings from 14:00.

gf_detail: Real, purpose-built GF items exist: a グルテンフリー塩ラーメン (gluten-free SHIO/salt ramen) using brown-rice noodles from Shimane, developed by the founder specifically with wheat-allergy and celiac diners in mind, plus vegan water-gyoza with a rice-flour wrapper (gluten-free available on request). The Tokyo Station Ichibangai and official listings note staff ask about wheat allergy and cook the GF order in a separate pot — a meaningful positive. HOWEVER this is a small 26-seat counter shop that simultaneously boils regular WHEAT ramen noodles, and the flagship 醤油らーめん is made with 生醤油 (wheat-based raw soy sauce); the standard broths/tsuyu and shared ladles/counter mean cross-contamination is possible. Choose the SHIO (salt) base, not shoyu. This is NOT a dedicated GF kitchen/fryer, so a strict celiac should confirm the separate-pot handling in person on the day and avoid any soy-sauce-based bowl.
vegan_detail: Several genuinely animal-free dishes: ヴィーガン担々麺 (vegan tantanmen — soy-milk/sesame broth with soy-meat crumbles and chili oil), a vegan veggie-soba (vegetable broth), ヴィーガン水餃子 (vegan water-gyoza, rice-flour wrapper), and a soy-milk soft-serve dessert. IMPORTANT caveats: the popular キノコベジソバ (mushroom veggie-soba) is only vegan when you ORDER IT WITHOUT the 鶏チャーシュー (chicken chashu) and mushroom oil — the default bowl is not vegan. The 貝塩らーめん (clam-salt ramen) is bonito- and shellfish-based — not vegan. Vegan items are served from roughly 10:00. Confirm no dashi/bonito when ordering, since the kitchen also runs animal broths.

cultural_comfort.note: Very tourist-accustomed location inside Tokyo Station Ichibangai's Ramen Street; English menus provided, English-language official website, ticket/counter service, no reservations, cash and IC transit cards only. Staff are used to allergy and vegan questions from foreign diners.

chef_bio.background: Founder of the Soranoiro group. Worked at Kumurasaki in the Shin-Yokohama Ramen Museum as a university student, then after a company job and a stint at Takechan Niboshi Ramen, joined Hakata Ippudo in March 2000 and trained across many departments for about 10 years 10 months (cooking, store operations, staff development). Opened the first Soranoiro in Kojimachi, Tokyo in June 2011. Now also works as a ramen consultant (frozen-noodle advisor, flour-company advisor, shop production and product development).
chef_bio.philosophy: Mission 'まだ見ぬお客様と業界の発展のために' (for customers yet unseen and the advancement of the industry). Carries the Ippudo principle '変わらないために変わり続けること' (to stay the same you must keep changing). Named the company from the Heart Sutra's 色即是空・空即是色. Sees himself as a chef, not just a ramen-shop operator, and deliberately gives each branch a different menu. Set out to make a ramen shop a woman could enter alone, and built vegetables into the noodles, broth and toppings.
chef_bio.specialty: Vegetable ramen (ベジソバ) — vegetables in the noodles, broth and toppings — plus vegan ramen and a gluten-free (brown-rice-noodle) ramen. The Soranoiro veggie/vegan soba was featured in the Michelin Guide Tokyo (Bib Gourmand, 2015–2017).

anecdotes.text: Trained about 10 years and 10 months at Hakata Ippudo (joined March 2000) before opening the first Soranoiro in Kojimachi in June 2011.
Developed the vegan ramen after a well-received appearance at Paris Ramen Week in 2014, building a vegetable-based broth enriched with carrot and red-pepper puree.

Over ~13 years has created around 300 seasonal limited ramen to connect diners with regional producers nationwide — including sustaining Sanriku seaweed purchases for 8 years to support post-tsunami recovery.

positives: Purpose-built gluten-free SHIO (salt) ramen using brown-rice noodles, developed by the founder specifically for wheat-allergy and celiac diners
Vegan water-gyoza with rice-flour wrapper; gluten-free version available on request
Official/Ichibangai listings state staff ask about wheat allergy and cook the order in a separate pot
English menus and a location very used to allergy and vegan requests
gf_cross_contamination: Small 26-seat counter that simultaneously boils regular wheat ramen noodles — shared water/ladles/counter surface
Flagship 醤油らーめん uses 生醤油 (wheat-based raw soy sauce); shoyu-based bowls and standard tsuyu carry wheat
Not a dedicated GF kitchen or fryer — separate-pot handling should be confirmed in person
soy_sauce_wheat: 醤油らーめん and other shoyu bowls use wheat-containing soy sauce; choose the salt (塩) GF base instead
vegan_cross_contact: Kitchen also runs chicken and pork/clam broths; the default キノコベジソバ includes chicken chashu and mushroom oil and must be ordered without them to be vegan
貝塩らーめん contains bonito and shellfish — confirm no dashi/bonito on any 'vegetable' bowl
staff_allergy_handling: Staff inquire about wheat allergy and reportedly use a separate cooking pot for the GF order; contamination risk still acknowledged

cuisine: Taiwanese oriental-vegan (台湾素食) café — 100% vegan & gluten-free cakes, rice-flour pizza, lu rou fan bowls
hours_raw: Weekdays 9:30–16:30; Weekends 9:30–17:00. Open year-round (無休). (Some listings show 10:00–20:30, but the official site states these shorter hours — confirm before a late visit.)

hours.notes: 無休 (open year-round) per official site; a few aggregator listings differ

gf_detail: This is one of the safest options in Tokyo for a celiac. The official site states the entire production kitchen is completely gluten-free ("すべてのメニューはグルテンフリー…製造のキッチンにも完全にグルテンフリー") and every menu item is wheat-free ("全てのメニューはグルテンフリー(小麦不使用)"). Cakes and pizza bases use 米粉 (rice flour); the signature rainbow cake is rice-flour, additive-free. Because the whole shop is GF (no wheat on premises), cross-contamination risk from shared flour/fryer is very low. One residual caution for a strict celiac: their savory Taiwanese dishes (e.g., 台湾ルーローハン丼 lu rou fan) are braised in soy-type sauce — Taiwanese vegan soy sauce can be wheat-based, so confirm the specific seasoning is GF tamari before ordering the savory bowls. The site's blanket GF claim covers this, but it is worth a one-line confirmation given the stakes.
vegan_detail: 100% vegan — "oriental vegan" (オリエンタルヴィーガン). Official site: no animal ingredients at all, no dairy, no eggs, no honey ("動物性の原材料一切不使用…乳製品、卵やはちみつも使ってない"). Additionally五葷抜き — free of the five pungent alliums (negi, garlic, nira/garlic-chives, rakkyo, asatsuki), following Taiwanese Buddhist素食 tradition. No hidden dashi or bonito: the cuisine is plant-based Taiwanese, and no fish/bonito stock is used. Cakes and dishes also contain no alcohol.

chef_bio.origin: Shanghai-born owner; her husband farmed organically in Taiwan and now devises the café's recipes
chef_bio.background: Iwahashi Haruka became unable to eat meat and, out of that struggle, founded a company importing vegan foods. She met her husband, who had been engaged in organic agriculture in Taiwan. Realizing that the素食 (vegetarian/vegan food) that is an everyday choice in Taiwan was almost impossible to find in Japan, she began cooking herself. The couple opened 松竹圓カフェ in December 2019 near Kappabashi in Nishi-Asakusa. (Note: one vegan-media profile describes the owner as Taiwanese; the more detailed Numero/Gnavi accounts describe her as Shanghai-born with a Taiwan-farming husband — reported here as the fuller version.)
chef_bio.philosophy: "自然食、ヴィーガン食の素晴らしさを多くの日本人に伝えたい" — to convey the wonder of natural, vegan food to many Japanese people. Faithful Taiwanese素食: fully plant-based and五葷-free (oriental vegan), ingredients carefully selected, each item made with heart ("原材料を厳選 一品一品に心を込めて").
chef_bio.specialty: Taiwanese oriental-vegan café fare: the 台湾ルーローハン丼 (plant-based lu rou fan) recreating braised-pork flavor without animal products; a seven-layer rainbow cake colored naturally with red koji, carrot, pumpkin, spinach, butterfly-pea and sweet potato on a rice-flour base; and rice-flour-base vegan pizza.

anecdotes.text: She recreates the braised-pork-belly lu rou fan — a dish traditionally built on pork — entirely animal-free while preserving its authentic Taiwanese taste; it is the shop's most popular savory item.
Visited exactly one year after opening (Dec 2020): despite COVID collapsing her ~80% foreign clientele, she said she came to value the deeper conversations with customers about why they eat vegan.
After being unable to eat meat, she turned that hardship into a vegan-food import business, then met her Taiwan-organic-farmer husband — the couple now develops the café's recipes together.

positives: Entire production kitchen is 100% gluten-free per the official site — no wheat handled on premises, so cross-contamination is inherently very low
Every menu item is both vegan and gluten-free; nothing on the menu contains wheat, dairy, egg, honey, or animal products
Cake and pizza bases use rice flour (米粉); rainbow cake is additive-free with natural plant colorings
Multilingual menus (Japanese / English / Chinese) make it easy to communicate needs
Also五葷-free (no garlic/onion family) — helpful for guests avoiding alliums
gf_cross_contamination: Whole shop is GF so shared-flour/fryer risk is minimal — but no explicit statement about a dedicated fryer was found
soy_sauce_wheat: Savory Taiwanese items (lu rou fan bowl) are braised in a soy-type sauce; confirm it is a wheat-free/GF tamari, as Taiwanese vegan soy sauce can be wheat-based
vegan_cross_contact: None — the establishment is fully vegan, no animal products anywhere
staff_allergy_handling: Owner is highly allergen-aware and personally driven by the vegan/GF mission; publishes GF/vegan FAQs in three languages

cultural_comfort.note: Multilingual menus and FAQs in Japanese, English and Chinese; a large share of clientele has historically been foreign visitors. A vegan/GF foreign diner can expect to be well understood.

cuisine: International cafe / world cuisine (curry, pancakes, sandwiches) with vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free and halal options
hours_raw: Open 24 hours, 365 days a year (attached to Sakura Hotel Jimbocho). Morning buffet 4:30–11:00; food service 11:30–21:00; drinks/alcohol served 24h.
gf_detail: The cafe markets "gluten-free pancakes" and lists gluten-free options, so at least one real GF item exists. But this is NOT a dedicated or GF-focused kitchen: it is a busy 24-hour international cafe attached to Sakura Hotel, cooking curry, buffalo wings, kebabs, sandwiches and pancakes in one shared kitchen with heavy wheat use (pancake/sandwich flour, fried items). No evidence of a dedicated GF fryer or separate prep area was found, and standard curries/sauces likely use wheat-based (koikuchi) soy sauce. A celiac should treat GF pancakes as a made-to-order item only and directly confirm cross-contamination handling, batter/soy-sauce ingredients, and fryer sharing before ordering. English-speaking staff and per-item allergen pictograms on some menu items help this conversation. Confidence: real options exist, celiac-grade safety unverified.
vegan_detail: Vegetarian and vegan options are advertised. Confirmed items from the menu include a vegetarian Falafel Sandwich (¥1,000) and a vegetarian beans curry; the kitchen also uses organic vegetables from a Tohoku farm. Note the signature "Sakura Curry" contains chicken, so specify the vegetarian beans/vegetable curry rather than the default. Verify curry bases and soups for hidden animal stock (chicken/dashi/bonito), and confirm falafel is fried in oil not shared with meat. As a mixed international cafe rather than a vegan kitchen, cross-contact with meat/dairy is likely; vegan items are available but not isolated.

cultural_comfort.note: Explicitly foreigner-friendly: attached to Sakura Hotel, which hosts guests from 100+ countries. Multilingual staff (English and Chinese), English/French/Spanish menus, English phone support (03-3261-3939), free Wi-Fi. A non-Japanese-speaking celiac/vegan diner can communicate needs here more easily than at most Tokyo restaurants.

gf_cross_contamination: Busy shared 24-hour kitchen cooking curry, buffalo wings, kebabs, sandwiches and pancakes together; high ambient wheat/flour use
GF pancakes appear to be a marketed option but no dedicated GF griddle/fryer/prep area was found in any source
Curries and sauces likely use wheat-based Japanese soy sauce; unverified
soy_sauce_wheat: Standard curries/sauces presumed to use wheat-containing koikuchi soy sauce; confirm before ordering
vegan_cross_contact: Meat and dairy cooked in the same kitchen; signature Sakura Curry contains chicken
Confirm falafel/vegetable items are not fried in shared meat oil
staff_allergy_handling: English-speaking, multilingual staff experienced with international guests
Per-item allergen pictograms shown on some menu items (e.g. chicken, dairy, root vegetables flagged)
positives: Openly markets gluten-free, vegetarian, vegan and halal options
Multilingual staff and English menu make allergy communication feasible
Some menu items carry allergen pictograms
Organic vegetables sourced from a Tohoku farm

chef_bio.background: No individual chef is publicly credited. Sakura Cafe Jimbocho is the ground-floor cafe of Sakura Hotel Jimbocho, part of the Sakura Hotel & Hostel group, which built its concept around affordable, foreigner-friendly hospitality for guests from 100+ countries. The food program is a group/brand concept (24-hour world-cuisine cafe) rather than a named-chef kitchen.
chef_bio.philosophy: Accessible, international, budget-friendly dining open around the clock, with deliberate accommodation of vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free and halal diets to welcome a global traveler clientele.
chef_bio.specialty: Sakura Curry, grilled-cheese curry, world-cuisine sandwiches and pancakes, international beers.

cuisine: Gluten-free Japanese / café (100% gluten-free kitchen, vegan-accommodating)
hours_raw: Open daily. Lunch 11:30–16:00 / Dinner 16:00–22:00 (last order 21:00). Tabelog lists 11:30–22:00 Mon–Sun; closed on public holidays. Opened 17 March 2026 on the former ROSY site. Tel 03-3527-1359 / hello.ohnana@gmail.com; reservations via TableCheck.

hours.note: Lunch 11:30–16:00 / Dinner 16:00–22:00 (LO 21:00). Closed on public holidays.

gf_detail: Genuine 100% gluten-free establishment — no wheat is used anywhere in the kitchen. The owner, Nana, has celiac disease and built the restaurant specifically so celiacs can eat every item without asking: the motto is "No need to ask — it's gluten free, all the time" (東京100％グルテンフリーレストラン). Because the whole facility is wheat-free, the usual Japanese wheat traps are removed: soy sauce/seasonings are the gluten-free type, there is no shared tempura/fry oil with wheat batter, and no flour dusting. This is one of the very few Tokyo spots a strict celiac can rely on without cross-contamination worry. No juwari/soba wheat-tsuyu concern applies here. (Verified against the restaurant's own site and Tabelog; if in doubt, staff ask about and double-check every allergy at ordering.)
vegan_detail: The restaurant's stated concept is "グルテンフリー100%・ヴィーガン対応" — gluten-free with vegan accommodation. A specific vegan menu was not published online at time of checking, and the food is Japanese-style, so hidden animal stock is the risk to flag: confirm that dashi/broths and sauces are made without bonito (katsuo), fish, or other animal products when ordering vegan. Staff proactively ask about all dietary restrictions and double-check the order, so vegan requests can be accommodated — but treat vegan dishes as made-to-request rather than a guaranteed dedicated vegan menu.

cultural_comfort.note: Built to welcome international tourists as well as Japanese diners; staff are reported to be friendly and English-speaking, and they walk through allergies with you. English-comfortable for a foreign celiac/vegan diner.

chef_bio.background: Founder and owner of Oh Nana!. She was diagnosed with celiac disease roughly four years ago and, after struggling to find safe food at restaurants, convenience stores and supermarkets across Japan, opened Oh Nana! in March 2026 — she frames it as Japan's first Western-standard, fully celiac-safe restaurant. The venue took over the site of the former organic restaurant ROSY near Kanda Station.
chef_bio.philosophy: Create an inclusive space where everyone — gluten-free or not — can share good Japanese food together and make happy memories, so that people with dietary restrictions no longer have to eat apart from family and friends. Guiding promise: 'No need to ask — it's gluten free, all the time.'
chef_bio.specialty: 100% gluten-free Japanese cuisine and café fare (lunch, café, dinner), plus gluten-free bento, gluten-free cooking classes, and a gluten-free food tour.

anecdotes.text: Nana was diagnosed with celiac disease about four years ago; unable to find safe options at Japanese restaurants, konbini or supermarkets and pained by not being able to share meals with family and friends, she saw on her travels abroad that celiacs can live freely — which inspired her to open Oh Nana!.
Her name Nana means 'seven' (a lucky number) in Japanese, and she was born on July 7th — the restaurant leans into that as a symbol of good fortune.
The restaurant's core promise to guests is 'No need to ask — it's gluten free, all the time,' reflecting her goal of a worry-free dining experience she couldn't find elsewhere in Japan.

positives: 100% gluten-free facility — no wheat used anywhere in the kitchen
Owner has celiac disease and designed the menu to be entirely celiac-safe
Staff ask about all allergies and double-check the order before finalizing (e.g. seafood, avocado, oat allergies noted)
English-speaking, tourist-friendly staff
gf_cross_contamination: Effectively none for gluten: the entire kitchen is wheat-free, so no shared-fryer, flour-dusting, or wheat-tsuyu cross-contact
soy_sauce_wheat: As a 100% gluten-free restaurant, soy sauce and seasonings are the gluten-free/tamari type rather than standard wheat shoyu
staff_allergy_handling: Proactively ask about all allergies/restrictions and double-check before serving; accommodate non-gluten allergies on request
vegan_cross_contact: Vegan is accommodated by request; confirm dashi/broths and sauces are free of bonito/fish stock when ordering vegan

cuisine: ヴィーガン・グルテンフリー野菜懐石（和食）
hours_raw: Lunch 11:30–14:00 (L.O. 12:30) / Dinner 17:30–22:30 (L.O. 20:30). Reservation-only (book by 12:00 the previous day; no same-day bookings). Closed Sundays, public holidays, and the last 2 days of each month.

hours.notes: Reservation-only; book by 12:00 the day before. Closed Sundays, public holidays, and the final 2 days of each month. Lunch L.O. 12:30, dinner L.O. 20:30.

gf_detail: The entire menu is a single reservation-only vegetable kaiseki course, and the official site states every dish is gluten-free as standard — this is not a soba shop, so no juwari-soba/wheat-tsuyu concern applies. The house dashi is built from kombu and vegetable trimmings only (no wheat, no animal stock), and chef Kawahara says he re-reviewed every seasoning for compatibility when converting the kitchen. Because 100% of the fixed course is served GF, wheat exposure is inherently low, but I could not find an explicit statement that the premises are wheat-free or that they use a certified gluten-free (tamari) soy sauce — so a strict celiac should confirm the soy sauce/seasoning base and cross-contact when booking. They accept allergy notes in advance ("if you have any allergies or foods you cannot eat, please tell us"), so flag celiac clearly at reservation.
vegan_detail: Fully plant-based by design — every course is vegan with no meat, fish, eggs or dairy. The critical hidden-dashi risk is eliminated here: rather than a bonito/katsuo dashi, chef Kawahara spent about a year developing an original kombu-and-vegetable-peel stock (distinct from traditional temple shojin-dashi) so the umami comes entirely from plants. Allium-free (no onion/garlic) versions are available with advance notice. No bonito, no hidden fish stock found in any source.

chef_bio.background: Career-changer chef: studied industrial chemistry at university and worked for a semiconductor manufacturer before switching to cooking at age 30. He enrolled at Hattori Nutrition College, then apprenticed for six years at Yanaka Uosaka, a kaiseki restaurant in Taito-ku (now closed), before opening Minoya in June 2008. For the first six years after opening he also rented and worked a farm in Koshigaya, Saitama to learn vegetables firsthand, closing it only when the workload became too much.
chef_bio.philosophy: Bring out the true character — aroma, texture and umami — of each seasonal vegetable using traditional washoku technique, so that a fully vegetable-based meal stands as authentic kaiseki rather than a compromise, and so that guests with dietary restrictions can share the same table as everyone else.
chef_bio.specialty: Monthly-rotating vegan, gluten-free vegetable kaiseki courses (25–30+ vegetables per course, under ~700 kcal) built on a house kombu-and-vegetable dashi; the menu never repeats the same dishes month to month.

anecdotes.text: He spent roughly a year independently researching to develop an acceptable kombu-and-vegetable-peel dashi, deliberately diverging from traditional shojin-dashi, then re-reviewed every seasoning and ingredient for vegan compatibility.
For the first six years after opening Minoya in 2008 he rented a farm in Koshigaya, Saitama and grew vegetables himself to deepen his understanding of produce.
He came to cooking late, leaving a semiconductor-industry job at 30 to train at Hattori Nutrition College and then apprentice six years at the kaiseki restaurant Yanaka Uosaka.

gf_cross_contamination: Entire fixed course is gluten-free, so no wheat dishes share the kitchen — but the site does not explicitly claim a wheat-free premises or a certified GF (tamari) soy sauce, so a strict celiac should confirm the soy-sauce/seasoning base at booking.
soy_sauce_wheat: Official site states all dishes are gluten-free; specific soy sauce type (tamari vs. wheat-based) not confirmed in sources — confirm when reserving.
vegan_cross_contact: Fully vegan kitchen; house dashi is kombu + vegetable only, no bonito/animal stock — cross-contact with animal products is inherently minimal.
staff_allergy_handling: Reservation-only with advance notice; site invites guests to state allergies or foods they cannot eat, and offers allium-free (no onion/garlic) accommodation on request.
positives: 100% vegan and 100% gluten-free menu by design
Original plant-based kombu/vegetable dashi replaces bonito dashi
Small 9-seat counter with open kitchen — easy to speak with the chef
English menu available

cultural_comfort.note: Bilingual/English menu is available and the restaurant actively welcomes international vegan and gluten-free diners, so ordering the set course is easy. It is a tiny 9-seat, reservation-only counter, so book by noon the previous day (web booking exists) and note dietary needs in advance; day-of conversational English fluency is not guaranteed but the fixed-course format keeps interaction simple.

cuisine: Plant-based vegetable izakaya (teppan-yaki野菜料理) — vegan & gluten-free-aware
hours_raw: Evening only, roughly 18:00–23:00 daily (L.O. food 22:00 / drinks 22:30). Cash only. Listings conflict on Saturday — hitosara shows open Mon–Sun incl. holidays, favy shows Saturday closed — confirm before a Saturday visit.
gf_detail: Genuinely strong GF setup for a Tokyo izakaya — but read the caveats. The house soy sauce is a gluten-free broad-bean (空豆) tamari-style shoyu, salt is Okinawan Nuchima-su, and cooking is advertised as roughly 98% non-oil on the teppan. The omakase vegetable course is described by the restaurant/Vegewel as 完全グルテンフリー (completely gluten-free), and the shop explicitly advertises accommodating グルテンフリー / ビーガン / 五葷抜き requests. It is NOT a dedicated GF kitchen: wheat lives on the premises — a Turkish simit/シミット sesame bread and a hummus set, plus an attached bakery whose ~30 breads are mostly wheat. Okonomiyaki uses 玄米・大和芋・米粉 (brown rice, yam, rice flour) as binder rather than wheat flour, but is cooked on the same teppan as bread items. A celiac should order the explicitly GF course, confirm the GF broad-bean soy sauce is used on their specific dishes, and flag cross-contact from bread/flour and the shared teppan. (No juwari-soba concern here — this is not a soba shop.)
vegan_detail: Plant-based vegetable izakaya (野菜居酒屋) with a dedicated vegan course (~¥3,500 pre-tax) and vegan-cheese (ビーガンチーズ) dishes — avocado/vegan-cheese spring rolls, vegan-cheese-baked gourd with oyster mushroom, strawberry & baby-greens okonomiyaki, hot teppan potato salad. Listed on Vegewel and Veganmania as a vegan destination, and 五葷抜き (no onion/garlic) is available on request. Dashi appears plant-based (no bonito/dashi-fish mentioned anywhere) but not explicitly confirmed — worth a check. The concept is framed as letting vegans and meat-lovers dine together comfortably (ビーガンの方と肉好きの方が), so confirm any individual dish is fully animal-free; the attached bakery also includes non-vegan breads (only ~1/3 of its breads are vegan).

chef_bio.background: Owner-chef who previously cooked at teppan-yaki (iron-griddle) restaurants before opening Genki. He has said he noticed that traditional teppan-yaki menus were surprisingly light on vegetables, which pushed him to open a vegetable-centred izakaya.
chef_bio.philosophy: Build an inclusive table where people with different dietary needs — vegan, gluten-free, five-pungent-free, and meat-lovers — can eat together without anyone feeling singled out, in a retro-modern space, using vegetables as the star and gluten-free broad-bean soy sauce plus near-oil-free cooking as the default.
chef_bio.specialty: Teppan-cooked vegetable dishes; the hot iron-griddle potato salad (玄氣のポテサラ) is the signature, alongside vegan-cheese-baked gourd and vegetable okonomiyaki bound with rice flour.

anecdotes.text: Niino came from the teppan-yaki world and opened Genki after realizing conventional teppan menus used surprisingly few vegetables, deciding to make vegetables the centerpiece instead.
He standardized a gluten-free broad-bean (空豆) soy sauce, Okinawan Nuchima-su salt, and ~98% non-oil cooking so that the whole kitchen leans naturally vegan and gluten-free.

soy_sauce_wheat: House soy sauce is a gluten-free broad-bean (空豆) tamari-style shoyu, not wheat-based — a genuine positive for celiacs, but confirm it is the sauce used on your specific dishes.
gf_cross_contamination: Wheat items share the premises: a Turkish simit/シミット sesame bread and hummus set, plus an attached bakery of ~30 mostly-wheat breads.
Teppan (iron griddle) is shared between GF vegetable dishes and bread/flour items — ask about cleaning/cross-contact.
Okonomiyaki is bound with 米粉 (rice flour) rather than wheat flour, but still cooked on the shared griddle.
vegan_cross_contact: Attached bakery includes non-vegan breads (only ~1/3 are vegan).
Shared teppan used for both vegan dishes and other items.
staff_allergy_handling: Restaurant explicitly advertises accommodating グルテンフリー / ビーガン / ベジタリアン / 五葷抜き requests, indicating allergy- and diet-aware staff; the omakase course is prepared 完全グルテンフリー on request.
positives: Gluten-free broad-bean soy sauce used as the house shoyu
Okinawan Nuchima-su salt; ~98% non-oil cooking
A vegetable omakase course billed as completely gluten-free
Openly handles vegan, gluten-free, and five-pungent-free needs

cultural_comfort.note: Foreigner-aware: listed on English-facing platforms (Tabelog EN, TripAdvisor, Vegewel) and used to explaining vegan/GF/five-pungent accommodations. A confirmed English menu is not documented, so expect some English plus gesture/translation help rather than fluent service — a written card of your needs (celiac + vegan) is wise. Cash only.

cuisine: ヴィーガン＆グルテンフリー 米粉焼き菓子・ブランチカフェ (vegan & gluten-free rice-flour bakery / brunch cafe)
hours_raw: Mon 9:30–16:30, Thu 10:30–16:30, Fri/Sat/Sun 9:30–16:30; closed Tue & Wed (per official site atomiyosowaka.jp). Note: launch-period press (Apr 2025) listed Mon/Thu/Fri 9:00–16:00 and Sat/Sun/holidays 9:00–17:00 — confirm current times on Instagram @atomiyosowaka_kuramae before visiting.
gf_detail: Effectively a dedicated gluten-free environment: the entire brand is wheat-free — no wheat flour is used anywhere in the operation. All baked goods and brunch items are built on 米粉 (rice flour from 四万十川源流の土佐れいほく米), JAS-certified oatmeal, domestic okara (soy pulp), and homemade apple yeast. The official site states products are suitable for wheat-allergy sufferers ("小麦アレルギー・卵アレルギーの方"). No tempura, no flour-dusting, no wheat soy-sauce tsuyu on premises (it is a bakery/brunch cafe, not a soba/noodle shop). CAVEAT for a strict celiac: the shop does NOT publish a formal cross-contamination protocol or third-party GF certification, and some items are co-produced with an outside welfare workshop (就労継続支援B型『ナンクルナイサァーろくえもん』) — that facility is also stated to make the vegan/GF sweets, but I could not verify its handling protocols. Oats are used (JAS oatmeal); highly oat-sensitive celiacs should ask whether the oats are certified GF-purity. Bottom line: no wheat is handled at all, which removes the primary celiac risk, but confirm oat sourcing and shared-equipment handling directly if you are highly sensitive.
vegan_detail: 100% plant-based. Official site: "バター、卵、牛乳などの動物性原材料は一切使用していません" (no animal-derived ingredients — butter, eggs, milk — ever used). Also avoids refined white sugar (uses agave syrup). No dashi/bonito concern: this is a baked-goods and brunch/bread-plate cafe, not a Japanese savory kitchen. Menu is entirely vegan: rice-flour muffins (cinnamon-roll, carrot cake, "milk"), cookies (orange-chocolate, almond, chai spice), banana bread, corn bread, carrot-spice bread, donuts, nut tarts, lemon/blueberry/kiwi cakes; drinks include Earl Grey, 日々乃コーラ craft cola, and specialty coffee from 田代珈琲. Whole facility is vegan, so no animal-product cross-contact risk.

chef_bio.background: Founder and representative (代表) of the operating company be.株式会社, headquartered in Osaka. She launched アトミヨソワカ in 2023 in Osaka's Taisho district (大正・泉尾) as a vegan & gluten-free baked-goods shop, and expanded to Tokyo with the Kuramae location, which opened April 29, 2025.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「ヴィーガン＆グルテンフリーをちゃんと美味しく」 — that dietary restriction is not compromise but the very source of a new kind of deliciousness. Three stated values: カラダにやさしく (kind to the body — accessible to those with allergies and dietary needs), ちゃんとおいしく (genuinely delicious), 地球にやさしく (kind to the earth — reducing food waste and single-use plastic). A core part of the mission is social: the sweets are co-produced with a 就労継続支援B型 welfare workshop (ナンクルナイサァーろくえもん), giving people who find it hard to work at ordinary companies a place to work at their own pace — 'sweets made not only to taste good but to bring joy to the people who make them.'
chef_bio.specialty: 米粉 (rice-flour) vegan & gluten-free焼き菓子 — muffins, cookies, banana/carrot-spice bread, tarts and cakes — plus a sit-down brunch bread plate. Signature sourcing: 四万十川源流の土佐れいほく米 rice flour, JAS-certified oatmeal and agave syrup, homemade apple yeast, domestic okara.

anecdotes.text: The name アトミヨソワカ comes from a Japanese good-luck charm/incantation said to help you find lost things (探し物が見つかるおまじないの言葉) — fitting the store's idea that a food-restricted diner will finally feel 'ここにあった' (it was here all along).
The Kuramae store's theme is 「実り」 (harvest/abundance): the interior centers on a symbolic tree salvaged from sustainable forestry, paired with secondhand furniture for a warm, nostalgic feel.
Part of the vegan/GF baking is made together with the 就労継続支援B型事業所『ナンクルナイサァーろくえもん』, tying the bakery to disability employment.

gf_cross_contamination: Entire facility is wheat-free — no wheat flour handled anywhere, which removes the main celiac risk.
No published formal cross-contamination protocol or GF certification; a strict celiac should confirm shared-equipment handling.
Uses JAS oatmeal — confirm oats are certified gluten-free-purity if you are oat-sensitive.
Some items co-produced with an external welfare workshop (ろくえもん); its handling protocols not independently verified.
staff_allergy_handling: Brand explicitly caters to wheat-allergy and egg-allergy diners and to vegans/food minorities ('小麦アレルギー・卵アレルギーの方、ヴィーガン、フードマイノリティの方').
positives: No wheat, egg, dairy, or refined white sugar used anywhere.
Fully vegan and gluten-free menu — every item is safe to order.
Rice-flour based; transparent about ingredient sourcing (Tosa Reihoku rice, JAS oats/agave, homemade apple yeast, domestic okara).
No preservatives.
vegan_cross_contact: None — the whole facility is 100% plant-based, so no animal-product cross-contact.

cultural_comfort.note: Small counter-and-cafe bakery in Kuramae popular with Tokyo's international plant-based crowd (featured in English on japanplantbased.com). Ordering is easy — pastries are displayed in a case and you point/choose. No confirmed English menu or English-speaking staff, but the visual bakery format and the explicitly allergy-aware, vegan/GF concept make it low-stress for a foreign diner. A few Japanese words or the Instagram help; 4-min walk from Kuramae Station (Toei Asakusa Line exits A4/A0).

cuisine: グルテンフリーカフェ / 米粉スイーツ (gluten-free café, rice-flour sweets)
hours_raw: IMPORTANT status flag: the 神泉町 (Shinsen-cho) 渋谷本店 is currently listed as 一時休業 (temporarily closed) and posted a 移転のお知らせ (relocation notice) on 2024-09-19 — confirm it is open and confirm the new location before visiting (tel 03-6416-1856 / Instagram @avan_sweets_ / avan-sweets.com). Historic hours at the old Shinsen-cho address varied by source: gnavi listed weekdays 8:00–21:00, weekends/holidays 9:00–21:00 (L.O. 20:30); other listings showed 11:00–19:00, 11:00–21:00 (L.O. 20:30), and 10:00–17:00. Reported closed day: Tuesday. Treat all of these as unverified and outdated.
gf_detail: Fully gluten-free specialist café: 小麦を一切使用しない — the entire kitchen uses zero wheat, substituting ultra-fine 米粉 (rice flour) from Yamagata Shonai "haenuki" rice plus rice oil, so there is effectively no wheat on the premises to cross-contaminate. Multiple profiles and a first-hand review note the shop contacts each manufacturer to confirm seasonings/ingredients contain no hidden wheat (調味料に隠れた見えない小麦), addressing the usual wheat-in-soy-sauce risk. Because the whole café is wheat-free, the fryer used for the gluten-free karaage/churros is inherently GF (not shared with wheat batter or flour dusting). NOTE: this is a sweets-forward café — many items also contain dairy and egg, which are separate allergen concerns, not gluten. Celiac caveat: the shop has relocated / is temporarily closed at the old address, so confirm the current location still runs the same all-wheat-free kitchen before relying on it.
vegan_detail: Not a vegan venue. Churros are made with rice flour and rice oil, and a few plain flavors (cinnamon-sugar, black-sugar, basil) may be closer to plant-based, but dairy and egg run through the menu: roll cakes use Hokkaido pure cream, the popular vanilla/chocolate "gluten-free ice cream" topping is dairy, financiers/madeleines/cheesecake/castella are butter- and egg-based, and the morning set is churros with scrambled eggs. Honey-butter churros contain honey and butter. No vegan labeling was found. A vegan diner should ask item-by-item and assume most sweets contain dairy and/or egg.

chef_bio.background: avan began as the original gluten-free sweets brand of a Shibuya café (サンテール渋谷 / Santé-le Shibuya) before growing into its own gluten-free café. The founder/owner (name not published in the sources found) is from the Shonai region of Yamagata Prefecture and sources the shop's signature ingredient — ultra-fine 米粉 from top-grade 'haenuki' rice — from their hometown, along with eggs from the foothills of sacred Mt. Gassan and local jizake (sake) syrup.
chef_bio.philosophy: A commitment to 'gluten-free living' that goes beyond avoiding wheat flour to chasing down the invisible wheat hidden in seasonings, verified manufacturer by manufacturer, so health-conscious and celiac guests can trust every ingredient. The name 'avan' is taken from the French 'avant' ('before') — the idea of offering a small, body-gentle happiness before your precious time. The Shibuya interior leans into a nature theme (greenery, running water) with Studio Ghibli books, soundtracks and merchandise.
chef_bio.specialty: Rice-flour churros (crisp outside, chewy inside; ~16 flavors incl. the signature chocolate 'Sweet Bear'), plus rice-flour financiers, roll cake, cheesecake, madeleine, castella, gluten-free afternoon tea, morning churros with scrambled eggs, and gluten-free karaage.

anecdotes.text: The owner is from Yamagata's Shonai region and deliberately uses the premium local 'haenuki' rice, milled into ultra-fine flour with rice oil, out of a wish to convey trustworthy ingredients to health-conscious customers.
The shop describes being 'thoroughly committed to gluten-free' by tackling the invisible wheat hidden in seasonings, contacting each manufacturer to confirm no wheat is used.
avan started as the in-house original sweets brand of Santé-le Shibuya, with churros made from Shonai 'haenuki' ultra-fine rice flour and rice oil, and eggs from the foothills of Mt. Gassan.

gf_cross_contamination: Entire café is wheat-free (小麦を一切使用しない), so there is no wheat flour, wheat batter or flour dusting on the premises to cross-contaminate — the strongest possible structural protection for a celiac.
Fried items (karaage, churros) are cooked in a kitchen with no wheat, so the fryer is inherently gluten-free rather than shared with wheat batter.
Residual risk is the relocation: the old Shinsen-cho kitchen is temporarily closed, so verify the new location maintains the same all-wheat-free setup.
soy_sauce_wheat: Shop states it checks seasonings for hidden wheat and contacts manufacturers to confirm none is used, which specifically targets the wheat-in-soy-sauce risk. Savory items are minimal (mostly sweets).
vegan_cross_contact: Dairy (Hokkaido cream, butter, ice cream) and egg are used throughout the sweets and morning menu; not suitable for strict dairy/egg-free without asking.
staff_allergy_handling: QR-code / tablet ordering and self-serve lemon water were reported; no specific account of staff allergy briefings was found. Because the whole menu is gluten-free by design, staff do not need to filter for wheat item-by-item.
positives: 100% wheat-free kitchen (dedicated gluten-free café).
Verifies seasonings/ingredients with manufacturers to rule out hidden wheat.
Rice flour sourced from owner's hometown (Yamagata Shonai 'haenuki'), rice oil used for frying.
Popular, well-reviewed among gluten-free diners and featured in Japanese GF café roundups.

cultural_comfort.note: Tourist-visited gluten-free café near Shibuya, featured in Japanese and travel media; Tabelog maintains an English listing. Ordering is via QR/tablet and the menu is visual (churros by flavor), which lowers the language barrier, but no confirmed English-speaking staff or English in-store menu was found. Expect basic Japanese to help; pointing and photos work. NOTE: confirm the shop is open at its new post-relocation location first.

cuisine: Vegan & gluten-free bakery-café + specialty coffee roastery
hours_raw: Daily 9:00–18:00 (open every day; no regular closed day listed)
gf_detail: Multiple independent sources (Vegewel, HappyCow, RETRIP, note.com, edo-create) agree that EVERY sweet/baked good on the menu is both vegan AND gluten-free — carrot cake, banana bread, oat cookies, and a vegan "cheesecake" made from soy-milk yogurt (豆乳ヨーグルト). No wheat-flour item was found anywhere on the food menu, so wheat cross-contact risk in the kitchen is inherently low. This is a bakery/café (baked goods + coffee), so there is no deep fryer, no tempura batter, and no wheat-soy-sauce tsuyu to worry about. However: no source documents a celiac-grade dedicated-GF protocol, and they bake on-site, so I stop at 'high' rather than 'dedicated'. A celiac should still confirm in person that flours/additives are certified GF and ask about shared bake equipment. Note there is NO soba here, so the juwari caveat does not apply. Drinks use plant milks (oat etc.); black coffee is naturally GF.
vegan_detail: Fully vegan café — self-described concept "All for green すべては自然のために." All drinks and desserts are 100% plant-based; only plant milks (oat, soy) are used for lattes; the "cheesecake" swaps dairy for soy-milk yogurt. Listed as vegan-certified on Vegewel. No animal products, and being a coffee/dessert café there is no fish dashi or bonito (katsuobushi) risk. Confirmed by Vegewel, HappyCow, RETRIP and note.com.

chef_bio.background: Founder of KIELO COFFEE, which he started in 2019 at age 23 in Akihabara; Be green by KIELO COFFEE in Hongo is the roastery/second location. Roasts in-house on a Giesen W6A (6kg) half-hot-air roaster.
chef_bio.philosophy: Operates under the concept 'All for green すべては自然のために' (everything for nature). Through the COVID-19 period he concluded that 'activities that are not environmentally correct cannot continue,' driving thorough sourcing choices — organic where possible, plant-based only, biodegradable takeout ware, and food-waste reduction (spent lemons from lemonade reused in muffins).
chef_bio.specialty: Light-roast, low-bitterness, fruity specialty coffee with fully traceable beans; sells ~6 single-origin varieties. Pairs the coffee with vegan + gluten-free baked goods.

anecdotes.text: Describes roasting as 'a fusion of science and art' (焙煎はサイエンスとアートの融合), designing roast profiles with a scientific approach to overturn the fixed idea that 'coffee is bitter.'
Founded KIELO COFFEE at just 23 years old in 2019 under the 'All for green' concept.
Says environmentally incorrect activity 'cannot continue,' a realization from the pandemic that shaped the shop's sustainable, plant-based, low-waste sourcing.

gf_cross_contamination: No deep fryer on premises — this is a bakery/coffee shop, not a fried-food kitchen, so no tempura-batter or shared-oil wheat risk.

Entire food menu is wheat-free/gluten-free, so kitchen-wide wheat exposure is inherently low; but baked goods are made on-site and no source confirms a certified dedicated-GF flour/equipment protocol — a celiac should verify in person.
soy_sauce_wheat: Not a savory/soy-sauce menu; no soba, no tsuyu, no obvious wheat-soy-sauce dishes found.
vegan_cross_contact: No animal products used anywhere; plant milks only, so dairy cross-contact is not a concern.
staff_allergy_handling: No documented formal allergy protocol; reviewers repeatedly describe staff as very friendly and knowledgeable, and English staff/menus are reported.
positives: 100% vegan menu (vegan-certified on Vegewel).
All sweets are both vegan and gluten-free per multiple independent sources.
No fryer and no wheat-based savory items reduce accidental-gluten pathways.
Plant milks only (oat/soy).

cultural_comfort.note: Vegewel lists English-speaking staff and English menus as available, and HappyCow reviewers (international visitors) call staff 'very friendly and knowledgeable' with positive experiences. Small roastery café, so English depth may vary, but a foreign diner should be able to order and ask about ingredients.

cuisine: Vegan / gluten-free (wheat-free) whole-food creative Japanese; also five-pungent-free (五葷抜き)
hours_raw: Closed Mondays. Tue: lunch 11:30–15:00 (L.O. 14:30). Wed–Fri: lunch 11:30–15:00 (L.O. 14:30), dinner 18:00–20:30 (L.O. 20:00, reservation-based). Sat/Sun: open from 10:00 (morning) through lunch, dinner reservation-based. Morning service (9:00–11:30) offered irregularly. Note: only beer / non-alcoholic beer contain wheat — all food is wheat-free. (Gnavi lists Tue closed; official site & Vegewel list Mon closed with Tue lunch-only — confirm before visiting.)
gf_detail: Rare fully wheat-free kitchen: the restaurant states 100% of its FOOD menu is gluten-free / 小麦不使用 (no wheat used anywhere in cooking), so cross-contamination risk from flour, tempura batter, or a shared fryer is minimal by design — this is why it's flagged for celiacs. Two caveats a celiac should still verify in person: (1) beer and non-alcoholic beer are the ONLY items on the premises containing wheat (beverages only, not used in cooking); (2) confirm the soy sauce/seasoning is gluten-free tamari — the "all food gluten-free" claim implies it, but I could not independently verify the soy-sauce brand from a fetched page. No juwari-soba involved here. Overall an unusually safe celiac option for Asakusa.
vegan_detail: 100% plant-based — the owner and all staff are vegan, so there is no hidden animal dashi, bonito (katsuo), fish sauce, egg, or dairy. Menu is also free of food additives and refined white sugar, and free of the five pungent vegetables (五葷: garlic, onion, leek, chives, shallot), making it suitable for Buddhist-style / oriental-vegetarian diners too. Lunch, morning, kids (up to age 7), sides, and reservation-based dinner all fully vegan. Takeout available on all in-store items.

chef_bio.background: Owner-chef. Formerly worked in the IT industry, then became a yoga instructor and dietary consultant. Discovered plant-based eating through the book 'Fit for Life,' which resolved chronic stomach pain she had had since middle school; became vegetarian in 2017 and fully vegan after reading a book on the realities of dairy and egg production, opening the restaurant about a year after going vegan. Has lived in Chiang Mai, Thailand and traveled extensively across Asia, Europe, and India.
chef_bio.philosophy: 'Veganism means being kind — to yourself, to animals, and to the planet.' She aims to introduce veganism gently through delicious food rather than confrontation, respecting that each person has their own timeline for dietary change; hence the 'Wellness Vegan' framing of food that is kind to body and soul.
chef_bio.specialty: Plant-based whole-food cooking that draws out natural ingredient flavors — additive-free, refined-sugar-free, wheat-free (gluten-free), and five-pungent-free.

anecdotes.text: She switched to plant-based eating to cure chronic stomach pain she had suffered since middle school, after reading 'Fit for Life.'
She and her entire staff are vegan, which she cites as why they can give attentive service to vegan and vegan-curious guests.

gf_cross_contamination: Only beer and non-alcoholic beer contain wheat (beverages, not used in cooking)
Soy sauce/tamari not independently verified as gluten-free — confirm in person
soy_sauce_wheat: Restaurant states all food is wheat-free, which implies GF tamari, but the specific soy-sauce product was not confirmed on any fetched page
vegan_cross_contact: None expected — kitchen is 100% plant-based with all-vegan staff, no animal products on premises
staff_allergy_handling: Dedicated allergy-information page linked from the menu
Owner and all staff are vegan and knowledgeable about ingredients
positives: Entire FOOD menu is wheat-free / gluten-free by design
Entirely plant-based, additive-free, refined-sugar-free
Five-pungent-free (五葷抜き)
English menu and English-speaking staff available

cuisine: Vegan / gluten-free Japanese kaiseki (野菜会席)
hours_raw: Lunch 11:30–14:00 (L.O. 12:30); Dinner 17:30–22:30 (L.O. 20:30). Reservation-only, both sessions — no same-day bookings (they prep only what the day's reservations need). Closed Sundays, national holidays, and the last 2 days of each month.

hours.notes: Also closed national holidays and the last 2 days of each month. Reservations must be made by the day before; same-day cancellation = 100% charge.

gf_detail: Explicitly markets a "ヴィーガン&グルテンフリーの本格和食コース." Owner-chef Kawahara spent ~a year rebuilding the kitchen's foundation for plant-based cooking and states he "systematically reviewed all seasonings and ingredients," and the vegetable course "がグルテンフリーにも対応できるようになりました" (can now be made gluten-free). Strong points for a celiac: it is a reservation-only, made-to-order 9-seat counter with no same-day service (nothing pre-batched), and GF is arranged as a deliberate advance accommodation rather than a substitution on the fly — so the kitchen knows in advance. IMPORTANT to confirm at booking: the site does NOT explicitly state that a wheat-free (tamari) soy sauce is used, and standard Japanese shoyu/mirin/miso and any wheat-containing seasoning is the main gluten risk in a course like this. When you reserve, state coeliac/セリアック and ask them to confirm wheat-free soy sauce (小麦不使用の醤油/たまり) and no wheat in any seasoning. No juwari-soba issue here — this is a vegetable kaiseki, not a soba shop. GF is request-based, so treat it as a confirmed accommodation you must arrange in advance, not a walk-in guarantee.
vegan_detail: A complete multi-course vegan kaiseki is offered (Vegetable Full Course ~12 items ¥9,500; Short Course ~8 items ¥5,500). Dashi is the key win: the site states "出汁は昆布と野菜のみで丁寧に取り、動物性のものは使用しておりません" (broth made only from kombu and vegetables; no animal products) — so no hidden bonito/katsuo dashi, which is the usual trap in Japanese vegetable cooking. No meat, fish, or eggs in the vegan course; monthly rotating seasonal-vegetable menu. Note: the restaurant ALSO runs a separate standard (non-vegan) 味農家 course that includes animal products, so it is not an all-vegan house — the vegan course is a distinct, fully plant-based menu you must order/reserve. Allium-free (五葷抜き) can be accommodated with advance notice.

chef_bio.background: Unusual second-career chef. Studied industrial/applied chemistry at university and worked in the semiconductor industry before changing course at age 30. He then enrolled at Hattori Nutrition College (服部栄養専門学校) and trained for about six years at a kaiseki restaurant in Yanaka before opening Minoya in June 2008. For roughly six years he also ran his own vegetable farm in Koshigaya, Saitama, to deepen his understanding of produce.
chef_bio.philosophy: Cook to 'draw out' (引き出す) each vegetable's own aroma, texture and umami through classical Japanese technique rather than mask it. He deliberately never repeats a course — the menu rotates monthly with the seasons so returning guests always get something new.
chef_bio.specialty: Vegan and gluten-free Japanese kaiseki built entirely from seasonal vegetables, anchored by a house dashi he developed over about a year from kombu and vegetable trimmings to replace fish-based stock. Roughly 30 vegetable ingredients per course, ~600 kcal total.

anecdotes.text: Kawahara started from a chemistry and semiconductor career, then pivoted at 30 to train at Hattori Nutrition College and a Yanaka kaiseki house before opening Minoya in 2008.

When he began building vegetarian menus around 2014 he found dashi the biggest obstacle — '和食の場合、一番のネックが出汁になります' — and spent about a year developing a custom kombu-and-vegetable-scrap dashi, then reviewed every seasoning, offering fully vegan-compatible kaiseki from 2017.
He kept his own vegetable farm in Koshigaya, Saitama for about six years and refuses to serve the same course twice, changing the menu monthly to keep regulars engaged.

gf_cross_contamination: Made-to-order, reservation-only kitchen with no same-day service — nothing is pre-batched, so a booked GF course is prepared deliberately for that guest.

Shared kitchen also produces a standard non-vegan/non-GF 味農家 course, so shared surfaces/utensils are a general (not disclosed as controlled) consideration — worth mentioning your coeliac needs explicitly when booking.
This is not a fried-food/tempura house, so shared-fryer batter risk is low, but no dedicated-fryer claim is made.
soy_sauce_wheat: Site does not confirm use of wheat-free (tamari) soy sauce; standard shoyu/mirin/miso and other wheat-containing seasonings are the primary gluten risk in a Japanese vegetable course — confirm '小麦不使用の醤油' at booking.
staff_allergy_handling: Accommodates gluten-free and allium-free (五葷抜き) requests with advance notice.
Chef states he systematically reviewed all seasonings/ingredients when building the plant-based menu.
Reservation-only with day-before confirmation gives the kitchen advance notice of dietary needs.
positives: Animal-free house dashi (kombu + vegetables only), no hidden bonito.
Kaiseki-trained owner-chef; small 9-seat counter, everything cooked to order.
Openly markets vegan + gluten-free and provides an English menu/website.
vegan_cross_contact: Separate standard course uses animal products; vegan course is a distinct menu — confirm you are booked onto the vegan/GF course.

cultural_comfort.note: Actively courts international vegan/GF travelers: English-language website and an English menu are provided, and web reservations are accepted (res-reserve.com / minoyavege.res@gmail.com). Spoken-English fluency isn't documented, but the written English support and foreign-guest focus mean a non-Japanese diner can reserve and dine comfortably. Reserve ahead — no walk-ins.

cuisine: マクロビ・ヴィーガン・グルテンフリー (unverified)
hours_raw: Unknown — no listing found.
gf_detail: UNVERIFIED. No website, Tabelog page, Vegewel/HappyCow entry, or any online footprint could be found for a restaurant named 五穀屋 玄米マクロビ食堂 in 南麻布/麻布十番. The cuisine signal (マクロビ・ヴィーガン・グルテンフリー) suggests a macrobiotic kitchen where GF is plausible, but nothing confirms a dedicated GF kitchen or fryer, and macrobiotic Japanese kitchens routinely use wheat-based shoyu/miso, wheat-thickened sauces, and seitan (pure wheat gluten). A celiac must NOT assume GF here. Confirm on the ground: ask whether shoyu is wheat-free tamari, whether any seitan/fu (wheat gluten) is used, and whether there is a shared fryer.
vegan_detail: UNVERIFIED. The マクロビ/ヴィーガン cuisine signal implies plant-based, and authentic macrobiotic cooking excludes animal products — but this could not be corroborated on any source. Even at plant-forward macrobiotic spots, watch for hidden bonito dashi in soups/simmered dishes (many "macro" kitchens still use katsuo dashi). Confirm the menu is fully plant-based and that dashi is kombu/shiitake only.

gf_cross_contamination: Unverified — no source found. Wheat-based shoyu, miso, and possible seitan/fu (wheat gluten) are standard in Japanese macrobiotic kitchens and are the primary celiac risks to check on-site.
soy_sauce_wheat: Assume standard wheat-containing shoyu unless staff confirm wheat-free tamari.
vegan_cross_contact: Check for bonito/katsuo dashi in soups and nimono.

cuisine: Ramen (煮干し・蛤の淡麗系そば／まぜそば)
hours_raw: DATA MISMATCH — see notes. For the actual むぎとオリーブ (Ginza main store): 11:00–21:30 (L.O.), closed Wednesdays; may close early when the soup sells out. Verify per branch.

hours.note: Ginza 銀座本店 hours: 11:00-21:30 L.O., closed Wed. No Sendagi/Nezu branch exists; approx pin in the seed record is unreliable.

gf_detail: NOT gluten-free — and this is NOT a gluten-free vegan bakery. むぎとオリーブ is a wheat-noodle ramen shop ("むぎ"/mugi literally means wheat). The core dishes (蛤SOBA / 鶏SOBA / トリプルSOBA / まぜそば) use wheat ramen noodles, and the broth/tare is built on soy sauce (wheat-containing shoyu) plus chicken, clam (hamaguri) and niboshi (dried sardine) stock. There are no米粉/gluten-free noodle options in any fetched source. A celiac cannot eat here. NOTE: the seed record's "ヴィーガンベーカリー・グルテンフリー" cuisine signal and the "千駄木駅徒歩4分" location appear to be scraped-in error — the real brand's branches are Ginza (本店), Nihonbashi, Saitama Shintoshin and Haneda T2 food court; no Nezu/Sendagi/Yanaka branch was found.
vegan_detail: Not vegan and not vegetarian. All signature bowls are built on animal stocks — chicken (鶏), clam/hamaguri (蛤) and niboshi/dried sardine (煮干し) — plus soy-sauce tare; the まぜそば/TKG style also uses egg. Hidden dashi/bonito is intrinsic, not incidental. No plant-based bowl is advertised in any source. A vegan cannot eat the ramen here.

chef_bio.background: むぎとオリーブ is a Tokyo ramen brand whose 銀座本店 (opened 2014, Ginza 6-12-12 銀座ステラビル 1F) earned a Michelin Guide Tokyo Bib Gourmand. It is known for a refined, non-typical-ramen-shop storefront and clam (蛤)/niboshi-forward 淡麗 soba. The specific founding chef's name was not verifiable from the fetched sources, so it is intentionally left blank rather than guessed.
chef_bio.specialty: 淡麗系 clam & niboshi shoyu soba, plus egg-and-olive-oil まぜそば.

anecdotes.text: The Ginza main store received a Bib Gourmand in the Michelin Guide (reported as 2015), a rare honor for a ramen shop, and is set on a back street behind GINZA SIX with an elegant, non-ramen-shop frontage.

chef_bio.philosophy: Rejects the idea of 'healthy ingredients' in favor of balanced variety and moderation. Ingredients are organic/low-pesticide vegetables, mechanically pressed rapeseed and extra-virgin olive oil only, Italian sea salt and cane sugar, domestic multigrain rice, everything handmade with no preservatives or chemical seasonings.
chef_bio.specialty: Build-your-own deli plate: multigrain rice and a large green salad (5+ leafy greens) with a choice of 2–4 house-made deli sides from a rotating case of 10+, plus house dressings.

cuisine: Soba (handmade buckwheat noodles) — Edo-style老舗, birthplace of kamo-seiro (duck seiro)
hours_raw: Mon–Fri 11:00–15:00 (L.O. 14:50) & 17:30–22:00 (L.O. 21:20); Sat 11:00–14:00 (L.O. 13:50); closed Sun, national holidays, and the 2nd & 4th Saturday of each month. (The restaurant's own site lists shorter dinner L.O. 21:00 and Mon–Fri only — call ahead: 03-3561-2647.)
gf_detail: Not gluten-free and not suitable for a celiac. This is a traditional Edo soba house: the noodles are a wheat-buckwheat blend (nihachi-style — no juwari/10-wari soba is advertised), so gluten is in the noodle itself. The house tsuyu (dipping/broth) is built on a katsuobushi/soda-katsuo/saba-bushi fish dashi combined with wheat-containing Japanese soy sauce (shoyu). There is no GF menu, no gluten-free soba, and no mention anywhere of allergen handling; a shared soba-boiling pot and shared prep with wheat items make cross-contamination unavoidable. Even a "plain" order would carry wheat via the noodles and the tsuyu. If a celiac still wants to visit, they must call ahead (03-3561-2647) — but treat this as a NO.
vegan_detail: No vegan menu and animal products are central. The signature dishes are duck (kamo-seiro / kamo course using Saitama domestic aigamo duck), and — critically — the tsuyu and soups on nearly everything are made from a fish-based ichiban dashi (bonito, soda-katsuo, mackerel/saba bushi), so hidden bonito/fish stock is in the "plain" soba broths too. The soba noodles themselves are wheat-and-buckwheat (plant-based as noodles), and there are vegetable side dishes (sakana/otsumami) and sake, but a strict vegan cannot rely on the dipping/broth. Would need to ask for a fish-free preparation, which is not standard here.

chef_bio.background: Ginza Chōjuan was founded in 1935 (Shōwa 10) and is run as a long-standing family soba shop. It belongs to the wider Chōjuan lineage of Edo soba houses that traces to Sōshichi, a Mikawa native who opened the first 'Chōjuan' in Kyōbashi Gorobei-chō around 1702–1704; over generations the master let promising apprentices go independent under the Chōjuan name, which is why many Chōjuan shops exist across Tokyo. This Ginza branch grinds its own buckwheat — grown on the family's own farmland in Hokkaido (Asahikawa) — on a stone mill in-house.
chef_bio.philosophy: House-grown, stone-milled Hokkaido buckwheat paired with a first-run (ichiban) dashi of katsuobushi, soda-katsuo and saba-bushi; the shop is proud of being the originator of kamo-seiro, letting rich domestic duck fat perfume the dipping broth.
chef_bio.specialty: Kamo-seiro (duck seiro) — the dish the shop claims to have invented — using domestic aigamo duck loin and thigh; also regional/craft sake.

anecdotes.text: The shop bills itself as the '90-year-old, birthplace-of-kamo-seiro long-established soba house' (創業90年 鴨せいろ発祥 老舗蕎麦屋).
It grinds buckwheat from its own farmland in Asahikawa, Hokkaido on a stone mill, and finishes dishes with a first dashi of bonito, soda-bonito and mackerel flakes.

The Chōjuan name dates to the Genroku era: Sōshichi came from Mikawa to Edo and opened the original Chōjuan in Kyōbashi around 1702–1704, with the lineage spreading as apprentices were set up under the same noren.

cuisine: Ramen — Tokushima style (soy-tonkotsu / 醤油とんこつ pork-bone-and-soy-sauce ramen)
hours_raw: Unverified. No Tokyo Station branch of Ramen Todai (ラーメン東大 / 株式会社東大) could be confirmed — the chain's own store directory, its Japanese Wikipedia entry, and Tabelog list only Tokushima, Kyoto (Kyoto Station), Shiga, Hyogo, Kagawa and Okayama outlets, and the Tokyo Ramen Street directory at Tokyo Station does not include Todai. Treat any hours as unknown until confirmed on site.
gf_detail: Not gluten-free and no GF options exist. Tokushima ramen at Todai is a wheat-noodle bowl in a rich soy-sauce-and-pork-bone (醤油とんこつ) broth — the broth is built on soy sauce, which is brewed with wheat, and the noodles are standard wheat chukamen. Signature toppings (simmered pork belly, seasoned menma, optional raw egg) sit in that wheat-soy broth, and diners are encouraged to add free rice, which does not change the wheat exposure. A celiac cannot safely eat here: wheat noodles + wheat-containing soy-sauce tare are unavoidable, and there is no dedicated GF preparation. Sources: tokushimakotomono.com review (describes it as 醤油とんこつベースのこってり系ラーメン, brown broth, pork belly, standard raw egg) and the official menu page.
vegan_detail: Not vegan or vegetarian. The core broth is pork-bone (とんこつ) simmered with soy sauce; the standard bowl is topped with simmered pork belly (豚バラ肉) and an optional free raw egg, both animal products. Even a plain bowl carries pork-bone dashi, so there is no hidden-dashi ambiguity to resolve — it is meat-based by design. No plant-based option is advertised.

chef_bio.background: 株式会社東大 (Todai Co., Ltd.) runs the Ramen Todai (ラーメン東大) chain, founded in Ōjin-chō, Tokushima City in April 1999, with the Daidō main store (大道本店) opening soon after. Per a Tokushima blog interview, the founder trained at the Tsuji Culinary Institute (辻調理師専門学校), apprenticed in Chinese restaurants at major hotels around Osaka Station, then worked at a large ramen chain before going independent in 1999; the surname 内藤 (Naitō) is cited for the president, but this is a single blog source and unconfirmed.
chef_bio.philosophy: The name 東大 was chosen to mean aiming for the very top (summit) of the ramen world — a play on the elite 'Todai' homonym expressing the ambition to reach the peak of ramen, not a link to Tokyo University. The company frames its mission as 'the evolution and cultural creation of Tokushima ramen' (徳島ラーメンの進化と文化創造).
chef_bio.specialty: Tokushima-style soy-tonkotsu ramen: a rich, dark brown soy-sauce-and-pork-bone broth with medium-thin noodles, sweet-savory simmered pork belly, seasoned menma, a free raw egg to crack in, and free rice on the side — the classic Tokushima 'ramen-with-rice' experience.

anecdotes.text: Won Grand Prix at the 2004 'Akashi Ramen Hatoba' event in Hyogo and the 2005 'Kuwana Ramen Kaidō' event in Mie, and took first place three years running (2005–2007) in the Tokushima town magazine Awawa's popular-ramen ranking.
A free raw egg cracked into the bowl is treated as standard for Tokushima ramen at Todai, and the shop leans into the local custom of eating the rich brown broth alongside white rice.

cuisine: ラーメン (vegetable ramen / vegan / gluten-free options)
hours_raw: 9:00–23:00 (L.O. 22:30). 年中無休 (open daily, no fixed closing day). Vegan and gluten-free bowls are served only from 10:00 onward.
gf_detail: A genuine gluten-free bowl exists: the Gluten-Free Shio (salt) Ramen (~¥1,300) swaps wheat noodles for brown-rice noodles made from Shimane Prefecture rice, and the official store page states the salt ramen is prepared wheat-free and boiled in a SEPARATE pot for allergy customers. Staff reportedly ask about celiac status when a GF order is placed (japanforkids.jp). Vegan/GF gyoza use rice-flour wrappers. Real celiac caveats remain: (1) this is a 26-seat wheat-noodle ramen counter — every other bowl uses wheat noodles, so airborne/utensil flour cross-contamination is possible even with a separate pot, and staff themselves acknowledge "cross-contamination is still possible"; (2) the kitchen uses brewed soy sauce (nama-shoyu from Oka Shoten, cited in the broth notes), which normally contains wheat — a strict celiac should confirm at the counter that the GF shio bowl's tare/seasoning is genuinely wheat-free and not the shoyu tare. Not a dedicated GF kitchen. Confirm celiac needs in person before ordering.
vegan_detail: Dedicated vegan bowls are on the permanent menu (available from 10:00): Vegan Tantanmen (soy-milk sesame broth, soy-meat crumbles, chili oil, tomato, mizuna) described on the official site as using "動物系食材を一切使わず" — no animal ingredients at all; Kinoko (mushroom) Vegi Soba with a mushroom + vegetable + soy-milk broth; the signature Veg Soba whose broth, paprika-colored noodles and toppings are vegetable-based (confirm the base Veg Soba vs. the explicitly-vegan version — the classic Veg Soba can contain animal stock, so ask for the vegan bowl by name). Also vegan gyoza (rice-flour wrappers) and vegan soy-milk soft serve. Hidden-animal risk: the shop also runs chicken (Amakusa Daio) and shellfish broths on the same line, so ask for the labeled "ビーガン/vegan" item specifically and confirm no bonito/chicken dashi in the bowl you order.

cultural_comfort.note: Very foreigner-friendly: multilingual menu (English/Chinese/Korean) that labels every dietary option, ticket-machine buttons for vegan items marked in English, inside Tokyo Station Ichibangai Ramen Street with heavy international traffic. Staff proactively ask about allergies.

chef_bio.background: Founder of the Soranoiro (ソラノイロ) group. Started ramen tasting as a high-schooler, then trained ~11 years under Ippudo (Chikaranomoto Company) and Gogyo before going independent, opening the first Soranoiro in Kojimachi, Chiyoda, in June 2011. Says he has eaten at 5,000+ ramen shops and created 200+ ramen recipes over a ~28-year career.
chef_bio.philosophy: Push ramen forward while keeping an orthodox chuka-soba as the flagship — pioneering vegetable-forward and animal-free bowls so that vegetarians, vegans and allergy/celiac diners can all eat ramen. Was among the first in Japan to put a gluten-free ramen on a permanent grand menu.
chef_bio.specialty: The Veg Soba (ベジソバ) — reputedly the first ramen to use vegetables across noodles, broth and toppings — plus vegan bowls and gluten-free ramen.

anecdotes.text: Developed Soranoiro's vegan ramen after a successful showing at Paris Ramen Week in 2014.
Soranoiro was listed in the Michelin Guide Tokyo 2015 Bib Gourmand, recognition for the innovative vegetable-based ramen.
Soranoiro is credited as one of the earliest shops in Japan to adopt gluten-free ramen onto its regular grand menu.

cuisine: 寝かせ玄米 (aged/fermented brown rice) teishoku & izakaya — healthy Japanese set meals
hours_raw: Lunch: weekdays 11:30–14:30 (L.O. 14:00), Sat/Sun/holidays 11:30–15:00 (L.O. 14:30). Dinner: 17:30–22:00 (food L.O. 21:00, drink L.O. 21:30), dinner closed Tue & Wed. Attached grocery/shop: Tue/Wed 11:30–15:00, other days 11:30–20:00. Tel 03-5829-9929.
gf_detail: Not a gluten-free restaurant — no GF program advertised. The signature 寝かせ玄米 (aged brown rice, cooked with adzuki beans and natural salt over ~3 days) is itself naturally gluten-free and is the safest core item; alternate rices (white, hijiki, zakkoku millet) are also offered. HOWEVER this is a full teishoku/izakaya kitchen where wheat is pervasive: the official menu prominently features 鰹出汁 (bonito dashi) in the rolled egg (tamagoyaki), plus soups and sauces that in a standard Japanese kitchen use regular wheat-containing soy sauce and mirin. A celiac would need to confirm each side dish and soup individually and ask them to hold soy-sauce-based seasoning. No dedicated fryer or GF soy sauce found. Treat as ASK, rely mainly on the plain brown rice.
vegan_detail: Not a vegan restaurant. Lunch teishoku lets you choose a rice (incl. brown rice), a meat OR fish main, plus side dishes, so a plant-forward plate is possible by picking vegetable sides. But animal products are core to the menu (meat/fish mains, bonito-dashi tamagoyaki, fish soups such as つみれ汁/鯛の粗汁, chicken chanko soup), and hidden 鰹 (bonito) dashi is very likely in the soups, simmered sides and seasonings. A vegan must explicitly confirm no dashi/bonito, no fish, no egg on each item. Some blogs describe it as vegan-adaptable, but there is no certified vegan set — treat as limited, confirm dashi.

cultural_comfort.note: Official site and in-store menus are Japanese-only; no English service advertised. It is a well-known, tourist-visited spot near Kuramae Station with picture-friendly teishoku, and staff are used to explaining the brown-rice concept, but a foreign diner should expect to point at photos or use a translation app and to spell out dietary needs (dashi/soy sauce/wheat) clearly in Japanese.

chef_bio.background: Founder and CEO of YUWAERU Inc. (株式会社結わえる), which he started in 2009 and whose Kuramae flagship (蔵前本店) opened as the company's home base. Before founding the company he worked at a major consulting firm on healthcare-related corporate consulting, where he grew convinced that lifestyle diseases were rising because of drastic changes in modern eating and living, and set out to build 'a world where people fundamentally don't get sick.' He styles himself the '玄米社長' (Brown Rice President) and a food & wellness researcher.
chef_bio.philosophy: The company name 結わえる means to 'tie/knot together' — bridging traditional Japanese living culture with modern life for a sustainable 21st-century lifestyle. His signature idea, 一日一膳 玄米生活 ('one bowl of brown rice a day'), centers on his 寝かせ玄米® (aged/fermented brown rice) as a complete staple food. He preaches achievable, non-perfectionist wellness — 'health at 70 points is fine' — rather than restrictive dieting, and links personal health to the health of the planet: choosing what you eat is choosing what future you want to live in.
chef_bio.specialty: 寝かせ玄米 (nekase genmai) — 100% brown rice slow-aged for about three days with adzuki beans and natural salt for a mochi-like, richer texture — served as balanced teishoku set meals alongside producer-direct seasonal ingredients and naturally-made sake.

anecdotes.text: Ogino founded YUWAERU in 2009 after leaving healthcare consulting, motivated by the conviction that most lifestyle diseases are preventable through everyday staple foods rather than medicine — which led him to research brown rice as a 'complete nutritious food.'

He argues restriction-based health approaches fail because they are unsustainable, promoting instead a 'simple dining table' of seasonal local ingredients and properly-made seasonings — captured in his line that you shouldn't have to give up alcohol or sweets to be healthy.
He frames the Kuramae shop's ambition as building a 'brown-rice theme park' that reconnects the present and past of Japanese food culture.
