cuisine: Vegan ramen / plant-based tantanmen (ヴィーガン担々麺)
hours_raw: 10:00–22:00 daily, open year-round (年中無休). Inside the ticket gates of JR Tokyo Station, so tied to station operating hours.

hours.notes: Year-round (年中無休). Located inside JR Tokyo Station Yaesu South gates, Gransta Tokyo 1F, Keiyo Street area.

gf_detail: Not safe for a celiac. T'sたんたん is a vegan RAMEN counter and its core noodle is standard wheat 中華麺 (Chinese-style wheat noodle) — gluten by definition. The tantan/soy tare is built on ordinary Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat, and the sesame-tantan base is a shared wheat-exposed kitchen. No dedicated gluten-free noodle, dedicated fryer, or gluten protocol was found for THIS Gransta Tokyo station location. Note: the brand's sister shop "T's Kitchen" (Ueno) and the flagship T's Restaurant in Jiyugaoka do advertise gluten-free noodle swaps / GF dishes, but that is a different address — do not assume the station stand offers it. A celiac should treat this location as wheat-based and, if they want to try the brand, go to the GF-equipped sister location instead.
vegan_detail: Fully plant-based — this is one of Tokyo's landmark vegan ramen shops. The entire menu uses no meat, seafood, dairy, or eggs ("肉・魚介・乳製品・卵を一切使わずに"), and the broth is a vegetable/kombu-style umami base rather than bonito/animal dashi, so there is no hidden fish-stock trap that plagues most Japanese ramen. Because the whole kitchen is vegan, there is essentially no animal cross-contact risk. An "oriental veg" (no onion/garlic, allium-free) option is also available. Confirm nothing is topped with honey-style condiments if you are strict, but the shop is designed and marketed as 100% vegan.

cultural_comfort.note: Very foreigner-friendly: inside JR Tokyo Station, high tourist traffic, and an English menu is available (英語メニュー). Vegan/vegetarian and allium-free options are clearly labeled. It is a fast, counter-style stand so interaction is brief, but a non-Japanese diner can order comfortably.

chef_bio.background: Founder and representative of T's Restaurant. Born March 1956, a Keio University graduate. She was originally a lover of animal foods (fatty tuna toro, cream dishes) and turned to plant-based eating after a close friend fell ill and was advised by doctors to cut animal products, which crystallized her belief in preventative health through everyday food. She opened the flagship T's Restaurant in Jiyugaoka in September 2009 and created the T'sたんたん vegan-ramen spin-off, which now runs multiple locations across Tokyo train stations and Narita Airport. She is a director of the Japan Plant-Based Market Association.
chef_bio.philosophy: 'Smile Veg' (スマイルベジ) — communicate the importance of health through food that is delicious enough that anyone, vegan or not, is happy to eat it. Vegan food should be an accessible, joyful default (in schools, offices, airlines, stations), not a compromise.
chef_bio.specialty: Vegan tantanmen and plant-based ramen with animal-free umami depth (no meat, fish, egg, dairy, or bonito dashi).

anecdotes.text: A former marbled-toro-and-cream lover, Shimokawa switched to plant-based cooking after a close friend became ill and doctors advised reducing animal products; she began serving her family tofu-based 'meat sauce' pasta and noticed her own mornings became lighter and more energetic.

T's Restaurant was born in a near-magical 5-day span in May 2009: a chance meeting with a photographer led to a plate designer who imagined a 'mountain-lodge-style' natural restaurant; the next day she spotted a newly built space near Jiyugaoka Station, called on impulse, and one unit was free. It opened on the 25th — a date she says kept recurring at every milestone.

Her vegan noodles were adopted as international-airline in-flight meals, and she published what is described as Japan's first home-use vegan recipe book, 『奇跡のごちそう』 (2013); her Smile Veg work has extended to corporate cafeterias and school lunches for tens of thousands of students in Tsukuba.

soy_sauce_wheat: The tantan/ramen tare is built on standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat.
No wheat-free (rice/tamari) soy sauce was documented for this station location.
gf_cross_contamination: Core product is wheat 中華麺 (wheat ramen noodle) — gluten by default.
Sesame/tantan base and boiling water are shared across an all-wheat-noodle kitchen.
No dedicated gluten-free noodle, dedicated fryer, or celiac protocol found for the Gransta Tokyo location.
vegan_cross_contact: Entire kitchen is 100% plant-based — no meat, fish, egg, or dairy on the premises, so animal cross-contact risk is essentially nil.
staff_allergy_handling: English menu available; vegan/vegetarian and allium-free (oriental veg) options are labeled.
Fast counter-style station shop — brief interaction, so confirm specifics before ordering if strict.
Parent brand (T's Restaurant) is allergy- and diet-aware, but station-counter staff allergy handling for gluten was not individually confirmed.
positives: Fully vegan kitchen — no animal-derived ingredients or bonito dashi, removing the usual hidden-fish-stock risk.
English menu and clearly labeled vegan / vegetarian / allium-free options.
Inside JR Tokyo Station (Gransta, Keiyo Street area) — easy, foreigner-friendly access.

cuisine: Vegan burgers (100% plant-based, Okinawa-origin)
hours_raw: Approx: Tue & Thu–Fri open until 22:00, Sat–Sun until 21:00 (opens ~11:00); closed Mondays (Retty also notes 不定休 / irregular closures). January–February the shop operates irregularly — the cafe explicitly asks diners to check its Instagram for current hours. WARNING: Tabelog and HappyCow both flag this location as closed as of 2026 — no separate closure announcement was found and it still appears on Uber Eats Tokyo / HotPepper, but confirm the shop is operating before making a trip.

hours.note: Semi-regular weekly pattern (Tue/Thu/Fri to 22:00, Sat/Sun to 21:00, closed Mon) but sources emphasize checking Instagram; Jan-Feb irregular. Possible permanent closure flagged on Tabelog/HappyCow 2026 - verify.

gf_detail: Not a gluten-free kitchen. The standard burger buns are made with domestic wheat flour (国産小麦), so the default burger is NOT gluten-free. A real GF option does exist: the teriyaki-avocado burger can be built on 玄米ライス (a brown-rice "bun") instead of the wheat bun, and some sides (e.g. potatoes) are described as gluten-free. Real celiac risks to confirm on-site: (1) the shop is a tiny ~5-seat counter with a single shared kitchen, so cross-contamination from wheat buns and flour handling is likely; (2) the teriyaki sauce almost certainly contains wheat-based soy sauce — ask before ordering the teriyaki burger even on the rice bun; (3) fry/griddle sharing with wheat items is unconfirmed. Treat GF here as "possible with care," not safe by default. English is limited, so bring a written GF/celiac card.
vegan_detail: Fully vegan (100%植物性) burger specialty — the entire menu is plant-based, so vegan cross-contact risk is low. Each patty blends 30+ ingredients (vegetables, grains, nuts, spices) with NO meat, NO soy meat (大豆ミート不使用), no animal products, no dairy, and no chemical seasonings/preservatives/colorings. The "cheese" and mayo are house-made from nuts, not dairy. Because it's an all-plant kitchen there is no bonito/dashi concern in the burgers; still confirm smoothies and any special sauces. Nut-heavy — a nut-allergic vegan should be cautious.

cultural_comfort.note: Small Okinawa-origin vegan cafe already popular with foreign tourists (a nearby business hotel sends guests) and listed on English platforms (HappyCow, Vegewel EN, Tabelog EN). Some English/menu help likely but not confirmed full English service; the counter is tiny (~5 seats). Bring a written GF card if celiac.

chef_bio.background: Earthful Cafe began as a popular vegan-burger cafe in Okinawa (the original delivers via Uber Eats in 北中城村/Kitanakagusuku); this Honjo/Kuramae location was its first Tokyo/mainland outpost, opening pre-open on 20 Dec 2023 and grand-opening around March 2024. The concept centers on burgers made only from vegetables and grains, deliberately avoiding soy meat, dairy and additives.
chef_bio.philosophy: 'ととのう' (feel restored/centered) through clean, additive-free plant food — a patty of 30+ whole ingredients rather than processed mock-meat, served in a pebble-floored, Okinawa-greenery-meets-Shinto-shrine space designed as an urban oasis.
chef_bio.specialty: 100% plant-based vegan burgers with a house nut-based cheese and mayo; a brown-rice-bun (玄米ライス) gluten-free variant of the teriyaki-avocado burger.

anecdotes.text: The interior is floored with pebbles and mixes Okinawan greenery with Shinto-shrine motifs to feel like an oasis in the city, framed around the idea of 'ととのう' (feeling restored).
Each patty uses over 30 kinds of vegetables, grains, nuts and spices and uses no soy meat, animal products, dairy, chemical seasonings, preservatives or colorings.
A July 2024 diner review praised the burger for a strikingly meat-like patty ('肉感すごいパティで、味もとっても美味しかった').

cuisine: Vegan / organic — Italian-French leaning plant-based (pasta, curry, burgers, katsu)
hours_raw: Lunch 11:45–15:00 (L.O. 14:30), Dinner 17:00–21:45 (L.O. 21:00). Nominally open daily, but since January 2025 they take irregular holidays announced on Instagram — confirm before going.

hours.note: Irregular holidays since Jan 2025, announced via Instagram; last orders lunch 14:30 / dinner 21:00

gf_detail: Not a GF-focused kitchen and NOT safe to treat as celiac-safe without asking. The restaurant does advertise a "gluten-free menu" and markets specific GF items — a chickpea-tomato stew billed as gluten-free and a gluten-free banana-coconut pound cake — so real GF dishes exist. But the core menu is wheat-heavy: the signature "katsu" is seitan (pure wheat gluten), plus pasta (arrabbiata/genovese/carbonara), a katsu sandwich, and breaded cutlets. Shared boiling pasta water, breading/flour dusting, and (likely) wheat-based soy sauce/sauces mean high cross-contamination risk in a single small kitchen with no evidence of a dedicated GF fryer or prep area. A celiac should order only the explicitly GF items and confirm in person that soy sauce/seasonings and prep are wheat-free. Being a vegan house, hidden dashi/bonito is not a concern, but wheat is the live risk here.
vegan_detail: Fully vegan restaurant — 100% plant-based, no animal products across the menu. Listed as a certified vegan venue on Japan VegeMap / NPO Veg Project Japan and on Vegewel. Opened Feb 2024 in Asakusa; positions itself as an accessible "entry point" to veganism via familiar comfort dishes (pasta, Japanese curry, lotus-root hamburg steak, seitan katsu, seasonal-vegetable pasta, brownies/mousse). Because the whole house is vegan there is no hidden bonito/fish dashi to worry about; dashi is plant-based (kombu/vegetable). Sake and wine served at dinner.

cultural_comfort.note: Vegewel lists English-speaking staff and an English menu; Tabelog carries an English page and online reservations. A foreign diner can expect to communicate dietary needs in English with reasonable ease.

chef_bio.background: The restaurant repeatedly states its menu is 'supervised by a French chef,' but no chef is named on the official BASE shop, Tabelog, Vegewel, VegeTime, or FindTokyoFood listings. The owner's stated aim is social contribution through 'food diversity' (食の多様性の一役を担いたい).
chef_bio.philosophy: Make vegan food that people crave and want to eat again (また食べたくなる味) rather than food defined by sacrifice; use familiar dishes as an accessible entry point to veganism for vegans and non-vegans alike.
chef_bio.specialty: French/Italian-leaning vegan comfort food — seitan katsu, pasta, Japanese vegan curry, lotus-root hamburg steak.

anecdotes.text: Opened in Asakusa in February 2024 and quickly earned a 4.7-star Google rating (100+ reviews within its first year), described as effectively the neighborhood's standout dedicated vegan restaurant.

cuisine: 湯葉・生麩の和食（京料理系）／懐石・会席
hours_raw: Lunch 11:30–15:00 (L.O. 14:00) / Dinner 17:00–22:30 (L.O. 22:00). Closed Sundays (日曜定休); Obon and year-end/New Year closures vary — confirm directly.
gf_detail: Not safe to rely on for celiac. The house specialty is 生麩 (nama-fu / raw wheat gluten), sourced from Kyoto's 半兵衛麩 — it is essentially pure wheat and appears throughout the signature dishes (生麩田楽, 生麩と季節野菜の揚げ出し, and the flagship 湯葉クリームコロッケ which packs yuba AND nama-fu into a flour-breaded, deep-fried croquette). Menu leans heavily on deep-fried items (揚げ湯葉サラダ, croquette, agedashi) with no indication of a dedicated fryer, so shared-oil and flour/panko cross-contamination is likely. Standard Japanese soy sauce and tsuyu (wheat-containing) and dashi season most dishes. A few items are naturally wheat-free in isolation (自家製豆腐, 湯葉 sashimi, vegetable obanzai) but there is no GF program, labeling, or allergen handling — a celiac should treat this as a wheat-forward kitchen. Note: any juwari/soba is not offered as a GF claim here regardless.
vegan_detail: Plant-forward but NOT a vegan/精進 restaurant — it is an omnivore washoku house that also serves wagyu (天草黒毛和牛). Genuinely plant-based components exist (湯葉 yuba sashimi/spring rolls, 生麩 nama-fu dengaku with miso, 自家製豆腐, vegetable おばんざい), but there is no vegan designation and hidden animal ingredients are very likely: katsuo (bonito) dashi in the 出汁茶漬け, ankake and simmered items; dairy/egg in the yuba cream croquette; wheat-based soy sauce. No 精進だし (kombu-only) is advertised. A vegan diner must explicitly ask each dish and request kombu dashi — do not assume the "vegetable" dishes are animal-free.

cultural_comfort.note: Traditional old-machiya washoku restaurant in Kagurazaka's Hyogo Yokocho alley; no English menu or English service is advertised on any listing. Expect Japanese-only. A translation app or a Japanese-speaking companion is advisable, especially for communicating vegan/gluten needs given the dashi and wheat-gluten issues.

chef_bio.background: 料理人になったきっかけは中学3年生の時、両親の行きつけだった小料理屋の板長の仕事に感銘を受け弟子入りを申し出たこと。浅草の料亭での修業に始まり、静岡や福島など各地の郷土料理に触れて研鑽を積む。東京に戻ってからは懐石の世界で腕を磨き、2020年4月より神楽坂おいしんぼ本店へ。
chef_bio.philosophy: 毎朝届く産地直送の食材の強みを最大限に生かし、真においしい食材を吟味し続けることに情熱を注ぐ。
chef_bio.specialty: 和食全般。京都・半兵衛麩から仕入れる湯葉・生麩を主役にした京料理系の一品料理と懐石。

cuisine: Vegan tsukemen / ramen (plant-based Japanese noodles)
hours_raw: Reported as Mon–Sat 11:30–23:00, closed Sundays (Hachidory); other listings show Tue–Sat 11:00–22:30 / Sun 11:00–22:00, closed Mondays. Vegewel notes irregular closures. Confirm before visiting. Cash only.
gf_detail: Not gluten-free. This is a wheat-noodle tsukemen/ramen shop: the house noodles are described as 全粒粉 (whole-wheat / whole-grain) high-hydration wheat noodles, so gluten is central to the dish. Toppings include lotus-root and pumpkin tempura (wheat batter) and the miso/soy-based broths almost certainly use wheat-containing soy sauce (shoyu). No dedicated GF kitchen, no GF noodle option was found in any source. A celiac cannot safely eat here.
vegan_detail: Plant-forward shop billed as the only vegan tsukemen/ramen in Suidobashi: broths use NO meat and NO fish/bonito dashi — umami is built entirely from concentrated vegetables (tomato-miso base for tsukemen, 100% soy-milk base for the tantanmen), with soy-meat (大豆ミート), lotus root, and pumpkin toppings. IMPORTANT caveat: the default house noodles contain egg (麺に卵が入ってしまってる, per Hachidory), and the standard tsukemen set comes with an egg 'uf mayo' (ウフマヨ) topping — so you must explicitly request vegan accommodation (egg-free) to eat fully vegan. A 五葷抜き (five-pungent-free) option exists for Buddhist/oriental-vegetarian diners. No hidden fish/animal dashi in the soups per multiple sources.

chef_bio.background: Came from an Italian-restaurant background before opening the shop (founded 15 Sep 2022). Not strictly vegetarian/vegan himself, but stopped eating meat for health and says his body felt noticeably better afterward ('肉を食べないようにしてから体調が良くなり、身体が楽になった').
chef_bio.philosophy: '罪悪感ゼロ' (zero-guilt) eating — a hearty, indulgent-tasting bowl that is nonetheless meat- and fish-free and lighter on the body. His Italian training shows in careful plating and presentation.
chef_bio.specialty: Vegetable-only concentrated tsukemen broth (tomato-miso) and 100% soy-milk tantanmen, with homemade whole-wheat noodles.

anecdotes.text: The manager previously worked in Italian cuisine and is meticulous about plating, producing a visually striking tsukemen with chewy, wholesome noodles.
He does not identify as vegan/vegetarian but limits meat for health, saying he felt better after cutting it out.

cuisine: Indian vegetarian (North & South Indian, Indo-Chinese) — plant-based-friendly
hours_raw: Daily 11:00–15:00 and 17:00–23:00 (無休 / open year-round, no regular closed day). Lunch offers free naan/rice refills.
gf_detail: Not a GF-focused or dedicated GF kitchen — treat as "some naturally GF items, ask carefully." Naturally gluten-free choices exist because much South Indian food here is rice/lentil based: dosa and idli are made from fermented rice + urad (black gram) batter, and plain rice, sambar, rassam, dal and most curries are wheat-free by tradition. REAL WHEAT RISKS to raise with staff: (1) naan, chapati/roti, paratha and puri are wheat — the kitchen dusts and rolls wheat flour in the same small space, so flour-dust cross-contact on other plates is plausible; (2) the Indo-Chinese section (chow mein / "chowmein", Manchurian, Hakka noodles) uses wheat noodles and wheat-based soy sauce; (3) samosa pastry is wheat and if it shares the fryer oil with pakora/bonda/vada, that oil is cross-contaminated — confirm whether the fryer is shared (unknown, see safety); (4) asafoetida (hing), a near-ubiquitous South Indian spice, is very commonly cut with wheat flour — a hidden gluten source in dal/sambar/chutneys that most staff won't flag unless asked directly. No juwari-soba issue here (not a soba shop). A celiac can likely eat well (rice + dal + plain dosa) but MUST ask about hing and the fryer; there is no allergen sheet evidence found.
vegan_detail: Establishment is 100% vegetarian (no meat, no fish, no egg) — so no hidden bonito/katsuo dashi or fish-sauce trap that plagues Japanese kitchens; this is Indian cooking. However it is LACTO-vegetarian, not vegan by default: paneer, ghee (clarified butter), butter, cream and yogurt/curd (and lassi) appear widely, and plain naan is typically brushed with butter/ghee. Vegan-safe items are marked with a green dot on the menu and staff will identify them, but you must ask. Reliable vegan picks reported: dosa and other rice/lentil dishes, dal, chana/aloo chana chaat, pani puri, baingan bharta, sambar/rassam, and "keema" made from soy mince / soy meatballs (大豆ミート). Confirm no ghee/cream/yogurt on the specific dish and ask for oil instead of ghee.

chef_bio.background: Family-run Indian vegetarian specialty restaurant that opened in 2014 in Taito-ku (east side of Okachimachi/Ueno). Indian-owned and operated, with Hindi spoken in-house and a following among the local Indian community. It has been selected multiple times (reported as six times) as a Tabelog Hyakumeiten (Top-100 curry) restaurant.
chef_bio.philosophy: '菜食中心' — vegetarian-centred Indian cooking that aims to satisfy as full Indian cuisine rather than as compromise 'veggie food'; no meat or fish used at all, with plant-based (vegan) options flagged on the menu.
chef_bio.specialty: South Indian dosa (notably an all-the-way crispy, パリパリ style, ~45cm) and thali/meals, alongside North Indian naan-and-curry and Indo-Chinese dishes; soy-'meat' keema.

anecdotes.text: A Tabelog Hyakumeiten (Top-100) regular, reported as selected six times since opening in 2014; its dosa is distinctive for a deliberately crunchy, entirely-crispy texture rather than the usual soft-and-crisp.

Covered as an 'インド菜食料理専門店' (Indian vegetarian specialty shop) whose food gives 'the satisfaction of having eaten Indian food, not just veg food' — soy-meat keema, latcha paratha, aloo bonda, pani puri and chai among the dishes.
Described in an Indian-curry writeup as a vegetarian-specialist 'detox curry' shop in Okachimachi, popular and recommended for its authentic meat-free cooking.

cuisine: リバーサイドカフェ／ヴィーガンスープ・ブレックファスト — vegan soup breakfast produced by the vegan brand GUGGA, served at the omnivore café CLANN BY THE RIVER (LYURO Tokyo Kiyosumi 2F)
hours_raw: Daily 7:00–22:00 (L.O. 21:00). The GUGGA vegan "soup breakfast" is served in the morning; menu also runs through lunch. Venue: CLANN BY THE RIVER, LYURO Tokyo Kiyosumi 2F.

hours.note: Soup breakfast served in the morning; same venue continues through lunch/dinner.

gf_detail: Important: "GUGGA" the brand is wheat-flour-free (its cookies/brownies use organic oat flour, no wheat), BUT this entry is the vegan SOUP BREAKFAST served inside CLANN BY THE RIVER, an omnivore riverside café at LYURO Tokyo Kiyosumi 2F — there is no dedicated GF kitchen or fryer. Concrete wheat risks found: (1) the soup breakfast is served with bread from Chigaya bakery OR rice — the bread is wheat; choose rice. (2) The seasonal vegan soup's seasoning/broth base (soy sauce, roux, stock) is not documented anywhere I could verify; standard Japanese shoyu contains wheat, so the soup itself is not confirmed GF. (3) The same kitchen prepares Kiyosumi clam chowder and BBQ-style dishes (venue inherited the PITMANS BBQ operation), so shared-surface cross-contamination is likely. Net: no GF assurance exists — a celiac must ask directly and treat as 'ask', not safe.
vegan_detail: Real, reliable vegan option: the "soup breakfast" offers a seasonal VEGAN soup as an explicit alternative to the KIYOSUMI clam chowder (the chowder contains dairy + clams and is NOT vegan). The vegan soup is produced by GUGGA, a fully plant-based sweets/recipe brand, so it should contain no bonito/dashi — but confirm the specific day's soup and side, since it is cooked in a shared omnivore kitchen. Sides are bread or rice (pick rice if avoiding egg/dairy in bread). This is NOT an all-vegan restaurant; it is an omnivore hotel café with a dependable vegan soup and GUGGA vegan baked goods.

cultural_comfort.note: Café inside LYURO Tokyo Kiyosumi (THE SHARE HOTELS), a design hotel used to international travelers, so expect at least basic English handling and likely some English menu support — but fluent allergy discussion is not guaranteed. Pointing to the 'vegan soup' vs 'clam chowder' distinction on the menu works well.

chef_bio.chef_name: 山後静音 (Shizune Yamago) — founder of GUGGA (brand that produces the vegan soup); the on-site cook at CLANN BY THE RIVER is not documented
chef_bio.background: GUGGA was founded in 2018 in Kamakura, Kanagawa. Shizune discovered veganism while studying at university in Hawaii, where her roommates were vegan, which reshaped how she saw plant-based food. She started GUGGA without a physical shop — catering, event pop-ups and wholesale — and it grew so popular through magazine features that a one-person operation could no longer keep up. She has since relocated to Kitanakagusuku Village, Okinawa, with her husband, who runs the chocolate workshop 'SANGO Bakes and Chocolate,' where GUGGA products are now based. GUGGA has no standalone Tokyo storefront; in Kiyosumi it appears as the GUGGA-produced vegan soup at CLANN BY THE RIVER.
chef_bio.philosophy: Reconstruct the American-style home desserts her grandmother used to bake with her, using 100% plant-based ingredients — wheat-flour-free (organic oat flour), domestic unrefined kibi cane sugar, organic coconut oil — so that 'vegan eating can feel this good' as an everyday reward rather than a restriction.
chef_bio.specialty: Vegan, wheat-flour-free soft cookies and sablés (flavors like espresso salted caramel, lemon-rosemary-macadamia, cranberry-chai-cacao-nib) and a 100% plant-based chocolate brownie; also develops vegan soups and recipes for partner cafés such as CLANN BY THE RIVER.

anecdotes.text: She discovered veganism as a university student in Hawaii, where all her roommates were vegan — the experience that led her to reimagine baked goods with only plant-based ingredients.

Demand outgrew what one person could bake; rather than 'stop production,' she built a network of collaborators and entrusts soft-cookie manufacturing to 'Aile Shonan,' a Type-B welfare work facility, maintaining quality through shared technical dialogue.
GUGGA has since moved from Kamakura to Okinawa (Kitanakagusuku), where products are sold at her husband's 'SANGO Bakes and Chocolate' workshop.

cuisine: ヴィーガン担々麺・ラーメン (100% plant-based tantan ramen)
hours_raw: Mon–Sat 10:00–22:00 / Sun & holidays 10:00–21:00. Located on 3F INSIDE the JR Ueno Station ticket gates (turn left after the Iriya/入谷 gate) — a platform/entry ticket (~¥150) is needed if you are not already travelling through the station. Reopened at this spot on 16 Oct 2025.
gf_detail: NOT safe for a celiac at this station outlet. The signature tantan ramen uses wheat Chinese-style noodles (中華麺 / non-fried wheat noodles), and the sesame-miso tantan tare is built on miso and soy sauce, which in Japan almost always contain wheat. T's own published allergen policy states plainly that "all menus are prepared using shared equipment and utensils together with other allergen-containing ingredients" and that they "cannot adjust cooking to accommodate an individual customer's allergy restrictions" — i.e. blanket wheat cross-contamination, no accommodation. The published allergen chart lists 小麦 (wheat) across the ramen line. The dedicated gluten-free rice-flour noodle option that Vegewel tags for the brand exists only at the full-service flagship (T's Restaurant, Jiyugaoka), NOT at this quick-serve Ecute Ueno station counter. A celiac should treat everything here as containing wheat. If you still want to try, ask (アレルギー表を見せてください／小麦は入っていますか) but do not rely on a safe answer.
vegan_detail: 100% vegan kitchen — the entire brand ("Smile-veg / スマイルベジ") uses no meat, seafood, eggs, or dairy anywhere on the premises. Broth and "meat" are built from soy milk, soy meat and vegetables; toppings like the "roasted-vegetable pork" and the "melted cheese" are soy-milk based. Because the whole kitchen is animal-free there is no hidden bonito/katsuo dashi or fish stock to worry about — a genuine relief point for vegans. Menu spans tantan ramen, yuzu shio ramen, soy-meat gyoza, soy karaage, curry and salads, all plant-based.

cultural_comfort.note: Long-standing destination for foreign vegan/vegetarian travellers; English menu and picture/photo menu available, ticket-style ordering, and staff used to non-Japanese diners. Being 100% vegan, you do not need to negotiate ingredients — the whole menu is safe for vegans without explanation. English help is limited but adequate to order.

chef_bio.chef_name: 下川祠左都 (Shimokawa Shizato) — founder, T's Restaurant / T's TanTan
chef_bio.background: A Tokyo homemaker who by her own account loved marbled toro, sirloin steak and other rich meat and dairy before founding the company. She had no professional culinary background; she taught herself plant-based cooking at home, e.g. using grated konnyaku to mimic ground meat, and refined dishes on her own family before opening a restaurant.
chef_bio.philosophy: 'Smile-veg' (スマイルベジ) — food should let everyone, whatever their diet, sit at the same table and say 'this is delicious' together. She frames health-through-food as prevention in daily eating rather than something you turn to only after falling ill, and wanted a welcoming shared space rather than merely a cookbook.
chef_bio.specialty: Vegan tantan-men (sesame-miso plant-based dan dan ramen) and the wider Smile-veg vegan menu; the brand's supervised 'Vegan Noodle' became an ANA international in-flight meal and expanded as T's TanTan into JR East stations.

anecdotes.text: The idea crystallised after a close friend fell ill and was told by doctors to cut out animal products; that pushed Shimokawa to see everyday diet as prevention and to devote herself to conveying 'the importance of health through food', which she named her life's work on 22 May 2009.

She began by making only dinner plant-based while leaving breakfast and lunch unrestricted, inventing tricks like grated-konnyaku 'mince'; her family's happy reactions convinced her the idea could work for non-vegans too.

Within five days in late May 2009 chance meetings with a photographer and a designer led her to the Jiyugaoka location and a team; strikingly, the logo approval (25 Jun), handover (25 Aug) and opening (25 Sep 2009) all landed on the 25th.

cuisine: South Indian (Tamil Nadu / Andhra / Kerala) — dosa, meals/thali, biryani; vegetarian-forward with meat options
hours_raw: Open daily 11:00–15:00 (L.O. 14:30) lunch, 17:00–23:00 (L.O. 22:30) dinner. No fixed weekly closing day; irregular closures over year-end/New Year and when at events. (Tabelog's English page lists slightly shorter hours of 11:00–14:30 / 17:00–22:30 — confirm on arrival.)

hours.notes: Lunch L.O. 14:30, dinner L.O. 22:30. No regular closed day; irregular closures at year-end/New Year and during events.

gf_detail: South Indian cuisine is one of the more naturally GF-friendly Indian styles: the house dosa, idli, vada batters and the sambar/rasam/vegetable curries here are rice- and lentil-based rather than wheat-based, and steamed rice + most curries carry no wheat by recipe. BUT this is NOT a dedicated or GF-aware kitchen and no GF program was found anywhere (official site, Tabelog, Gurunavi). Concrete wheat risks a celiac must clear before ordering: (1) the menu also serves wheat breads — naan, chapati/roti and poori/puri (the special-meals set even comes WITH puri) — cooked in the same kitchen, so flour is airborne and on surfaces; (2) asafoetida (hing), used routinely in South Indian tempering (tadka) of sambar/dals/vegetable curries, is very commonly cut with WHEAT FLOUR — this is a classic hidden-gluten trap and there is no confirmation the brand they use is wheat-free; (3) vada, bonda, pakora and poori share a deep fryer with battered/wheat items; (4) some curry gravies and Indo-Chinese-style items (e.g. Manchurian) can contain wheat flour or wheat-based soy sauce. Treat as 'options, verify': good chance of a safe rice/dosa/rice-based-curry meal, but a celiac must explicitly confirm no-asafoetida (or wheat-free hing), no shared-fryer items, and no thickener before relying on it.
vegan_detail: Genuinely strong vegan potential for an omnivore restaurant: as authentic South Indian, they run a full vegetarian side (vegetarian thali ¥2000, vada, sambar, plain/masala/Mysore/onion-rava dosa, aloo gobi, bhindi masala, vegetable curry) and many of these are plant-based by recipe. However dairy is used freely in the kitchen and it is NOT a vegan restaurant: raita/lassi (yogurt), paneer dishes, and — critically — GHEE (clarified butter) is a standard South Indian cooking fat and is often brushed on dosa and stirred into dal/curries; some naan/breads use dairy. There is no vegan labelling on the menu. So: order vegetable/lentil dishes and dosa, but explicitly ask for no ghee/no butter/no paneer/no dairy on each item. No bonito/dashi risk (this is Indian, not Japanese food), so the hidden-animal concern here is dairy/ghee, not fish stock.

cultural_comfort.note: Foreigner-comfortable: full official English website and English menu, an English Tabelog page, listed on the Chiyoda tourism site and in a Japan Muslim/halal guide, and Indian floor staff who generally speak English. Two-floor, ~80-seat casual restaurant a 5-min walk from Suidobashi Station (also ~5 min from Jimbocho Exit A4). Accepts Visa/Master.

chef_bio.background: Sri Balaji is a small Tokyo group: the original branch opened in Nakameguro in 2007–2008 and this Suidobashi branch (its second) opened in August 2015; combined the two seat ~100. The company states its cooks are South Indian career chefs: 'Our chefs are from South India with a rich experience, from very famous hotels in Tamil Nadu where they have been serving traditional authentic south Indian food for many number of years.'
chef_bio.philosophy: To introduce traditionally rich, authentic South Indian cuisine (Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala) to diners in Japan, and to let guests 'enjoy authentic south Indian food in a friendly and relaxed atmosphere.'
chef_bio.specialty: Tamil-Nadu-style South Indian: dosas (masala, Mysore masala, onion rava, Sri Balaji special), tiffin/meals and thali, sambar and vada, plus biryani and non-veg curries.

anecdotes.text: Credited by an English guide with helping bring then-lesser-known South Indian cuisine to prominence in Tokyo since its 2007 Nakameguro debut, expanding to Suidobashi in 2015.

A Japanese review notes the Suidobashi branch opened August 2015 as the second location, seats ~80 over two floors in beige/light-brown tones, with staff described as 親切 (kind/attentive); the reviewer observed the lunch meals set omits サンバル (sambar), a small concession to mainstream tastes.

gf_cross_contamination: Not a GF-aware kitchen; no gluten-free program found on the official site, Tabelog or Gurunavi.
Wheat breads (naan, chapati/roti, poori/puri) are made in the same kitchen — the special-meals set is even served with puri — so flour is present on surfaces and airborne.
Asafoetida (hing) used in South Indian tempering is commonly diluted with wheat flour: a hidden-gluten risk in sambar, dal and vegetable curries unless confirmed wheat-free.
Shared deep fryer for vada/bonda/pakora and poori (battered/wheat items).
Possible wheat-flour thickeners in some gravies and wheat/soy in any Indo-Chinese 'Manchurian'-style dishes.
soy_sauce_wheat: Core South Indian dishes do not use soy sauce, but any Indo-Chinese menu items (e.g. Gobi Manchurian, hakka noodles) may use wheat-based soy sauce — ask if ordering those.
vegan_cross_contact: Ghee (clarified butter) is a standard cooking fat — often on dosa and in dal/curries; ask for no ghee/butter.
Dairy used throughout: paneer, yogurt (raita/lassi), and butter/cream in some gravies and breads.
staff_allergy_handling: No documented allergy protocol; South Indian staff generally speak English, so dietary requests (no ghee, no dairy, no wheat/asafoetida) can be communicated directly — but treat all avoidances as best-effort, not guaranteed.
positives: Naturally rice-and-lentil-based South Indian core (dosa, idli, sambar, rice, vegetable curries) gives real GF and vegan starting points uncommon in North-Indian-heavy menus.
Dedicated vegetarian menu/thali and staff accustomed to vegetarian requests.

cuisine: Pure-vegetarian Indian (South Indian meals/dosa + Gujarati & Rajasthani thali), Jain-adaptable; no meat, fish or egg
hours_raw: Lunch 11:15–15:00 (L.O. 14:30) / Dinner 17:15–23:00 (L.O. 22:30). Open daily, no regular closures (無休). Lunch is cash-only.

hours.notes: Lunch L.O. 14:30, dinner L.O. 22:30; open daily (無休); lunch is cash-only

gf_detail: Fully vegetarian Indian kitchen, so none of the usual Japanese wheat traps: no soy sauce, no tsuyu, no tempura, no soba. Naturally gluten-free choices are real and plentiful — plain rice, South Indian meals, dosa and idli (rice + urad-lentil batter), sambar, rasam and most vegetable/lentil curries. BUT this is NOT a gluten-free-safe kitchen: wheat breads (naan, chapati, paratha, puri, methi thepla) are made and flour-dusted in the same prep area, and Indian asafoetida (hing) — used in many dals and vegetable dishes — is very commonly cut with wheat flour, a hidden gluten source a celiac must confirm dish-by-dish. No dedicated GF kitchen, fryer or stated GF protocol was found. A celiac should ask for asafoetida-free / flour-free preparation and stick to rice-based dishes.
vegan_detail: Lacto-vegetarian by default. The whole restaurant is free of meat, fish and egg (owner is a Jain practitioner), so there is zero hidden bonito/dashi or meat-broth risk — unusually safe for vegans in Japan. However dairy is used heavily: ghee, paneer (palak paneer, paneer tikka masala), yogurt and lassi. The menu explicitly carries a 'Vegan' category alongside Vegetarian and Jain, and the owner adapts dishes to each diner ('some won't eat onions, others will — we make food to match each person'). Naturally-vegan picks include South Indian meals, dosa/idli, sambar, rasam and many bean and vegetable curries cooked in oil rather than ghee. Ask for vegan (no ghee/paneer/yogurt); if you also avoid onion/garlic, request the Jain version.

cultural_comfort.note: English menu available; Indian owner/staff, halal-certified and long accustomed to foreign vegetarian, vegan and Muslim diners. English is workable though staff fluency varies — pointing at the menu's Vegan / Jain / Vegetarian labels works reliably.

chef_bio.chef_name: Rajendra Jain (ラジェンドラ・ジェイン)
chef_bio.background: Indian jewelry merchant and Jain practitioner based in Okachimachi. He opened Veg Herb Saga on 21 December 2009 to give the area's large community of Jain gem traders — who dominate India's diamond and gem-cutting trade and have done business in Okachimachi's jewelry town for decades — a place where they could actually eat out under strict Jain dietary rules.
chef_bio.philosophy: Rooted in Jain ahimsa (non-violence): pure vegetarian with no meat, fish or egg, and no root vegetables such as onion, garlic and potato (uprooting them harms soil life), plus avoidance of vegetables prone to insects. Rather than a fixed menu he cooks to the diner's own beliefs, offering parallel Jain (no onion/garlic) and non-Jain versions of the same dish, alongside vegetarian and vegan options.
chef_bio.specialty: Regional pure-veg thalis rarely found in Tokyo — Gujarati thali (Surat-nu-Jaman) and Rajasthani thali — plus South Indian meals, dosa, and the signature bean-and-herb 'veg kebab'.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant exists because Okachimachi grew into a jewelry town where most Indian gem dealers are Jains, and it is often described as the one place strict Jains in Tokyo can eat out.
Rajendra says he cooks to each person's convictions: 'Some won't eat onions, others will. No matter how busy we are, we take the request and make a different dish.'

The kitchen makes true Jain and non-Jain versions of the same dish — e.g. the Jain paneer tikka masala drops onion (keeping tomato and cashew) for a lighter result, while the non-Jain version adds onion and yogurt.

The official allergy page (moukotanmen-nakamoto.com/allergy) explicitly lists 小麦 (wheat) among 31 allergens and states 「調理の際、アレルギー物質を含むメニューと共通の調理器具を使用しております」 (shared cooking equipment is used across all menu items), so cross-contamination is guaranteed even for any lower-gluten item. Wheat risks confirmed: wheat ramen noodles, miso/辛味噌ダレ and soy-based tare that contain wheat and soybeans (小麦・大豆 listed), and a shared pot/utensil line. There is no dedicated GF menu, kitchen, or preparation. Celiac travelers should avoid.
vegan_detail: Despite the "vegetable tanmen" appearance and a heavy cabbage/vegetable topping, this is NOT vegan-safe. The signature soup is an animal-based spicy miso broth: ingredient breakdowns and the official allergen list confirm pork extract/lard (ポーク・豚肉) plus ground pork (豚ひき肉) on the 蒙古タンメン, and the allergen roster also includes 鶏肉 (chicken), ゼラチン (gelatin), 卵 (egg), 乳 (dairy) and さば/さけ (mackerel/salmon) across the menu. Shared cooking equipment across all items means unavoidable animal cross-contact even for the most vegetable-forward bowls. No official vegan or vegetarian option was found on the menu or allergen pages. The seed's "ヴィーガン対応" signal appears to be an error — treat as not vegan.

chef_bio.chef_name: 白根誠 (Makoto Shirane) — current owner/president; founder 中本正 (Tadashi Nakamoto, 1937–2014)
chef_bio.background: The shop's predecessor, 中国料理中本, opened in September 1968 near Kami-Itabashi Station, founded by 中本正 (originally as a borscht-serving eatery, ボルシチの店 中本). Nakamoto pursued intensely spicy dishes rarely seen in other restaurants at the time. The shop closed in December 1998 for the founder's health. A devoted customer of ~20 years, 白根誠, repeatedly asked to inherit the shop, was refused, then trained under Nakamoto and reopened it as 蒙古タンメン中本 in 2000. It is now operated by Shirane's company, 株式会社誠フードサービス, across multiple Tokyo/Kanto branches.
chef_bio.philosophy: Faithfully carry on and refine founder Nakamoto's 辛うま (spicy-yet-delicious) flavor, built on a miso-and-chili base with a 0–10 spice scale so each diner picks their heat.
chef_bio.specialty: 蒙古タンメン (spicy miso vegetable tanmen) and the fiery 北極ラーメン; a regional spicy-ramen institution.

anecdotes.text: The chain began in 1968 as 中本正's small Kami-Itabashi eatery — reportedly starting with borscht (ボルシチの店 中本) — where he pursued spicy dishes rarely found elsewhere.

When the original shop closed in 1998 for the founder's health, longtime regular 白根誠 — who had eaten there for ~20 years — begged to take it over, was turned down repeatedly, then apprenticed under Nakamoto and revived it as 蒙古タンメン中本 in 2000.
Today the branches are run by Shirane's 株式会社誠フードサービス, which grew the once-single shop into one of Tokyo's best-known spicy-ramen chains.

Shared cooking equipment guarantees animal cross-contact even for vegetable-forward bowls.

cuisine: Vegan izakaya (plant-based Japanese pub food — karaage, gyoza, small plates)
hours_raw: Daily 12:00–22:00 (lunch sets 12:00–15:00; dinner 15:00–22:00; last order food 21:00, drinks 21:30). Closes only when Shibuya PARCO closes.

gf_detail: This is an all-VEGAN but decidedly wheat-heavy izakaya — it is not a safe bet for a celiac. The signature dishes are the problem: the vegan karaage is 大豆ミート (soy meat, which is typically wheat-gluten-bound) deep-fried in a flour batter, and the vegan gyoza use standard wheat-flour dumpling wrappers. Standard Japanese soy sauce and izakaya seasonings contain wheat, and there is a shared deep fryer for the battered items. No page (PARCO shop page, Tabelog, or diner reviews) mentions gluten-free options, wheat-free tamari, a dedicated fryer, or celiac accommodation. Treat as 'no' for a strict celiac; at most, ask staff whether any single small plate (a plain vegetable dish) can be made without soy sauce, but assume cross-contamination.
vegan_detail: Fully plant-based establishment — billed as Japan's first vegan izakaya. The kitchen states it uses only plant-based ingredients, no meat, egg, or dairy, so there is no hidden bonito/katsuo dashi or fish stock risk. Signature items are all vegan recreations: karaage from soy meat with five sauces (daikon, black vinegar, Sichuan mala, mayo, etc.), gyoza, tartar sauce made from pumpkin, and 'ebi chili' made from konnyaku. Reviewers note the plant-based recreations are convincingly meat-like. Excellent choice for vegans; the caution is gluten, not animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: Strongly inbound/tourist-oriented and used to foreign vegans — the PARCO shop page and Tabelog have English versions, and a diner reported the room was dominated by English-speaking customers with a multilingual service environment. A foreign diner should be comfortable ordering here.

chef_bio.background: Ownership/chef not publicly named in the sources found. The venue is presented as Japan's first vegan izakaya, opened inside Shibuya PARCO B1F and framed around inbound (international-visitor) food culture, pairing retro 'red lantern' izakaya aesthetics with plant-based versions of pub classics. The owner curated a photo series of Tokyo slopes displayed near the west elevator, each with a short philosophical message — a play on the shop name 真さか (masaka / 坂 'slope').
chef_bio.philosophy: Make familiar Japanese izakaya comfort food — karaage, gyoza, lemon sours — fully plant-based and welcoming to vegans and non-vegans alike, so international and local diners can share the same table.
chef_bio.specialty: Vegan karaage (soy-meat) with multiple sauces; vegan gyoza; lemon sour.

cuisine: Ramen (creative / vegan tantanmen; wagyu & chicken paitan)
hours_raw: Daily 11:30–23:00 (last order 22:00). Irregular holidays follow Shibuya PARCO's closure calendar. (Shibuya PARCO B1F lists building hours 11:00–23:00.)
gf_detail: Not safe for celiac. This is a wheat-noodle ramen shop — every bowl, including the vegan tantanmen and vegan miso ramen, is served over standard wheat (komugi) ramen noodles. No gluten-free noodle option is offered. The shop's own menu lists gluten as one of the flagged allergens (alongside pork and egg), confirming wheat is present. The vegan tantanmen sauce and broths are made with soy sauce and sesame/nut pastes that typically contain wheat-brewed shoyu. A celiac cannot eat the ramen here; treat as gluten-containing. (Verdict is 'no' rather than 'ask' because wheat noodles are unavoidable in the core product.)
vegan_detail: Genuine, clearly-marked vegan options at an otherwise omnivore ramen shop (the house specialty is A5-wagyu and chicken-paitan ramen). Vegan menu includes: vegan tantanmen (with soup) and soupless vegan tantanmen, vegan miso ramen (regular and spicy), and a vegan "Garlic Knock Out" ramen, plus vegan rice/veg sides. Reviewers and the shop note every item is marked vegan-or-not, and the marked vegan broths are plant-based (no meat/chicken stock). No explicit bonito/katsuo dashi warning surfaced, and MENSHO's vegan line is intentionally animal-free — but because this is a shared kitchen also cooking wagyu/chicken, confirm "no dashi, no fish" (だし・かつお不使用) when ordering. Staff are described as accommodating and there is an English menu.

chef_bio.background: Self-taught ramen creator and founder of the MENSHO group. He studied business administration at Sanno University but left after ~2.5 years, worked in construction to save startup capital, and opened his first shop, Menya Shono, in Ichigaya (Shinjuku, Tokyo) in 2005 at age 25. He deliberately did not apprentice at an existing ramen shop, teaching himself to avoid being bound by convention. MENSHO has since grown to roughly 33 locations across six countries (Japan, USA, Australia, China, Thailand, Singapore); the San Francisco outpost earned Michelin recognition. Jikasei MENSHO is his Shibuya PARCO shop built around a WAGYU × RAMEN concept alongside a dedicated vegan line.
chef_bio.philosophy: Ramen as a vehicle for happiness and boundary-pushing creativity. After cooking large-scale relief meals following the 2011 Tohoku earthquake, Shono resolved to bring happiness to people around the world through ramen. He is known for constantly inventing 'creative ramen,' and for building a broad plant-based menu so vegan, vegetarian and international diners can share the same table.
chef_bio.specialty: Creative and 'jikasei' (house-made) noodles; A5-wagyu and chicken-paitan bowls, and a signature vegan tantanmen line.

anecdotes.text: Shono developed roughly 100 varieties of original 'creative ramen' within about five years, releasing new inventions on a monthly basis — he had been experimenting with pork-bone soup at home since high school.
He is self-taught: rather than train under an established master, he chose to learn ramen-making on his own to avoid being confined by the conventions of existing shops.

After leading large-scale relief cooking following the 2011 Tohoku disaster, he decided to bring happiness to people worldwide through ramen — a mission that drove MENSHO's international expansion to six countries.

BUT this is NOT a dedicated gluten-free kitchen. The same kitchen fries 大豆ミートのから揚げ (soy-meat karaage) and other 揚げ物, and bakes 天然酵母のパン (wheat natural-yeast bread) on premises, so shared-fryer and airborne-flour cross-contamination are real. Standard 醤油 (wheat-containing shoyu) is the likely base for the karaage marinade and sauces, and the vegetable demi-glace may be thickened with wheat flour — none of this is confirmed gluten-free. A celiac should ask staff to identify which specific dishes are GF, confirm tamari vs wheat soy sauce, and confirm the fryer is not shared with battered/breaded items before relying on it.
vegan_detail: Fully vegan restaurant — 100% plant-based, Ayurveda-informed, "肉や魚を一切使わず" (no meat or fish at all). Every menu item is animal-free, including a vegetable-only demi-glace, soy-milk dressing, natural-yeast bread and a vegan (lactose-free) cheesecake; no fish/bonito dashi is used (stocks are plant-based). Signature dishes: vegan ハンバーグ (burger), 大豆ミートのから揚げ (soy-meat karaage), 完熟ゆり根のポワレ, brown-rice pasta and seasonal vegetable courses built on 熟成野菜 (aged vegetables). Also advertised as chemical-seasoning-free / additive-free.

chef_bio.background: Vegan chef who trained at restaurants in 20+ countries before opening his own vegan restaurant in 東高円寺 (Higashi-Koenji), Tokyo in 2009, then launched PEACE TABLE in Shibuya Dogenzaka (opened 1 June 2020). Described in Japanese vegan media as ヴィーガン界の巨匠 ('a master of the vegan world').
chef_bio.philosophy: Believes the next stage of vegan cuisine is not meat/fish substitutes but fully drawing out vegetables' own deliciousness — 'ヴィーガン料理の新たなステージは、肉や魚の代替品ではなく、野菜料理本来のおいしさを味わい尽くすための料理'. Concept: a vegan restaurant that satisfies non-vegetarians, rivaling Michelin-starred cooking without any animal products.
chef_bio.specialty: Aged-vegetable (熟成野菜) vegan cuisine — vegetables aged in soil/snow for months up to two years, sourced mainly from Hokkaido and Awaji Island; signature vegan hamburg with a vegetable-based demi-glace.

gf_detail: Real, structured GF accommodation but NOT a dedicated GF kitchen. The reservation platform (TableCheck) lists a gluten-free set where the normally wheat-containing items are swapped to gluten-free versions — tempura, kabayaki (eel-style), yakiniku and tuna-mayo — which implies gluten-free/tamari soy sauce and a GF batter are used for that set. Wheat risks to confirm when booking: (1) standard sushi is served pre-brushed/pre-seasoned, so the default seasoning is regular wheat-based shoyu unless you have the GF set — good news is you never dip soy sauce yourself, but confirm the brushed nikiri/tare on your pieces is the GF version; (2) the regular tempura and kabayaki use wheat batter/sauce, so the same kitchen and likely the same fryer handle wheat — ask about a dedicated fryer / separate prep for the GF tempura, as none is confirmed; (3) plant-based "eel"/"meat"/egg mock items can contain wheat gluten (seitan/soy-wheat protein) in their non-GF form. Net: genuinely celiac-friendly by intent and several celiac guests report a good experience, but treat it as shared-kitchen GF — reserve the GF set and re-confirm tamari + no cross-contact on arrival.
vegan_detail: 100% plant-based — Japan's first all-vegan sushi specialty restaurant. Everything from the sushi to the miso soup, pickles and dessert (matcha ice cream) is vegan. Menu spans vegetable nigiri (eggplant, myoga, kinako) plus plant-based "seafood" (mock shrimp tempura, plant tuna, plant roe), vegan egg and plant meat. Sets ~¥3,000–6,000; sets are customizable (a reviewer swapped out mushrooms), so allergen/preference substitutions are workable.
